articles.title: Zelenskyy says Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russia will intensify war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia as a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.
The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”
In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.
“We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”
In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
The act, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.
“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”
The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”
The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Zelenskyy also said the military-grade Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces still had limited functionality, and would disconnect from the network when travelling at more than 161km/h (100mph), interfering with drone operations.
The service was throttled inside Ukraine without warning on Tuesday, and Zelenskyy said his government had determined that the restrictions were a “deliberate operation … to prevent us from defending ourselves”.
 
By sending vehicles with the terminals into EU countries, the Ukrainians found they operated at speeds of more than 180km/h, in effect proving that the terminals were only experiencing restrictions in Ukraine.
 
“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union,” he said. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Trump’s announcement that he would pause US sanctions came a week after he said Washington had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, in addition to the White House reportedly ordering the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces.
“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.
He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.
“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

articles.title: F-16s Down Majority of Jet Drones Amid Munition Build-Up, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Combat aviation, primarily Western-supplied F-16 multirole fighter jets, accounts for 55 to 60 percent of all intercepts against Russian turbojet-powered Shahed strike drones as Ukraine scales up stockpiles of 20mm aircraft ammunition, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
He explained that Ukraine has expanded procurement contracts to supply F-16 squadrons with the 20mm cannon rounds required to engage high-speed aerial threats, noting that deliveries have reached stable volumes.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Regarding the interception of jet-powered Shaheds, we are using our aviation very successfully,” Zelensky stated. “Today there is a build-up of ammunition for F-16s with 20mm shells. Both I and our Ministry of Defense had agreements. Right now we are receiving an appropriate quantity, and it is very good. That is, right now we have this.”
The Ukrainian head of state emphasized that combat aviation represents one pillar of a multi-tiered counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) posture, designed to mitigate disruptions caused by bandwidth restrictions on satellite-guided drone platforms.
“Next, we have several other solutions. Inexpensive missiles that are beginning to work,” Zelensky said.
“Several new solutions that will arrive in Ukraine from partners shortly, alongside domestic production that is already functional. Furthermore, we have turrets, and as you know, we began manufacturing them – not in isolated units, but in dozens. We will continue to scale them up.”
Major Russian Strike on Vinnytsia Region Injures 6
European Patriot packages and the FREYJA anti-ballistic initiative
Addressing the defense against Russian ballistic missiles, Zelensky stated that Ukraine requires an immediate transitional package of Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors from European partner nations to safeguard critical municipal infrastructure ahead of winter.
The president outlined a sequential air defense roadmap under which European transfers will bridge the gap until bilateral procurement contracts with Germany and the multilateral FREYJA anti-ballistic missile project become fully operational.
“Right now a package is needed from Europe and from certain other nations,” Zelensky explained.
“Next, our contracts with Germany and FREYJA should begin operating in parallel. This is the plan, these are my calculations.”
Zelensky observed that Ukrainian defense planners have identified European partner countries that maintain sufficient interceptor inventories, noting that deliveries through the NATO-coordinated PURL program have been constrained because the majority of US-manufactured PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors have been redirected to combat operations in the Middle East.
“Partners heard all our concerns,” Zelensky said.
“They know the quantities we receive through the PURL program and understand that the majority of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from the United States went to the Middle East. They know that I need their support right now.”
Zelensky confirmed that development work is progressing on the FREYJA anti-ballistic system, a 10-nation cooperative initiative involving key partners such as France and Norway.
While acknowledging that sovereign ballistic missile defense systems historically require decades to formulate, Zelensky emphasized that the strategic timetable requires accelerated engineering schedules.
“Regarding the FREYJA anti-ballistic project, Ukraine has done what it needed to do. What the partners need to do – 10 countries are participating – is in progress,” Zelensky noted, adding that he reviewed the program during bilateral consultations with French President Emmanuel Macron.
“Systems like this are worked on for decades. We want this very quickly, because there is no time.”
Push for European satellite autonomy following Starlink speed caps
The technical adjustments across Ukrainian air defenses unfold following disclosures earlier on Saturday that Starlink satellite terminals operating inside Ukraine have been subjected to an artificial velocity cap of 161 km/h (100 mph), disabling domestic unmanned interceptors designed to pursue turbojet loitering munitions.
Zelensky revealed that comparative trials conducted by Ukrainian specialists confirmed that Starlink-equipped vehicles operated normally at speeds of 180 km/h (112 mph) within EU borders, demonstrating that the operational constraints were geographically confined to Ukrainian territory.
The unilateral throttling has prompted European governments to examine sovereign alternatives to commercial American satellite communications networks, Zelensky observed.
“All of Europe saw that it is possible to regulate Starlink from the United States, regardless of agreements and contracts, and to limit speeds,” Zelensky said. “Therefore, Europeans themselves are now raising the issue of analogues. And they are already working on this.”
Ukrainian defense officials have stressed that diversifying air defense munitions, scaling domestic automated gun turrets, and establishing independent European satellite communications frameworks remain vital to preserving municipal utility grids and civilian population centers ahead of freezing winter conditions.

articles.title: Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
Zelensky’s diesel-fueled burnout
This week did not start well for Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, who was apparently blindsided by US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies after talks with the Kremlin. The deal won’t alleviate the global diesel shortage, but it’s already cooling speculative markets and easing pressure on Trump ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
For Zelensky, it’s a “diplomatic nightmare,” as Russian analyst Sergey Poletaev wrote for RT. Trump rubbed salt in the wound on Saturday when he openly suggested that Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal” and halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump went on to claim, “wants to make a deal more than Zelensky.”
Backed into a corner, Zelensky began throwing haymakers. Accusing the American president of empathizing with dictators, Zelensky demanded air defense missiles from the US before vowing to continue his drone campaign against Russia’s refineries – with or without American support.
The US apparently sent a warning signal to Zelensky by throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to SpaceX’s high-speed Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services, which are vital tools in guiding attack drones used against Russia, and in detecting incoming retaliatory strikes. Neither Trump nor SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would take responsibility for the communications drop-off, but even if they had, their message would likely have fallen of deaf ears.
Zelensky escalates the energy war
The Ukrainian leader followed through on his promise to keep hitting Russian refineries, despite Trump’s announcement of an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kiev (which neither side confirmed). Ukrainian forces attacked facilities in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions on Wednesday, before firing a barrage of four long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing kamikaze drones at the Ryazan refinery again on Thursday.
Debris from an intercepted UAV triggered an intense fire at the facility, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.
Retaliation was swift, from both Moscow and Washington. Russian forces used missiles and drones to strike six power plants in Kiev, Kharkov, and the surrounding regions, as well as military logistics hubs and data centers. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, confirming reports that Zelensky launched the refinery strikes knowing Ukraine lacked adequate air defense supplies to repel the retaliation.
Trump went on to savage Zelensky in a Newsmax interview on Thursday. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country,” he said, before accusing the Ukrainian leader of selling missiles given to him by the US “on the open market.”
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump concluded.
Nord Stream trial begins
As Ukraine doubles down on its infrastructure war, the costliest infrastructure attack in history is finally being litigated in a German courtroom. Sergey Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer, went on trial in Hamburg this week, accused of leading the team that sabotaged the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in September 2022, an act that German prosecutors consider a “war crime.”
Kuznetsov is staying silent, refusing to admit or deny a role in the bombing. The evidence against him is circumstantial, and his lawyers are confident that without a confession, he “cannot be convicted.”
As RT has explored in depth, the prosecution’s version of events is riddled with plot holes and inconsistencies. However, to pick apart the alternative story – that the pipelines were destroyed in a CIA operation – would call the relationship between Washington and Berlin, the foundation of the postwar liberal order, into question.
While a guilty verdict against Kuznetsov would directly implicate the Ukrainian military in a war crime against its largest foreign donor, the trial, at least at this stage, appears set up to avoid this outcome.
Russiagate resurrected
Speaking of reopening old wounds, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham dug up the bloated corpse of ‘Russiagate’ this week to bolster his efforts to undo the 2016 Brexit referendum and rejoin the EU. Burnham claimed that he had “clear” evidence that Russia interfered in the vote, in which Britons voted by 51.89% to 48.11% to leave the union.
Just as the original ‘Russiagate’ claims against Trump fell apart under questioning, Burnham’s allegation crumbled once subjected to some basic scrutiny. The British PM was unable to back up his accusation when grilled in Parliament, and his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, humiliated himself on national television when he attempted to evade questioning on the claim.
The final nail in the coffin came when Burnham’s own domestic intelligence chief cautioned against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
However, Burnham couldn’t be faulted for his timing and opportunism. As he spoke of Russian bots and influence campaigns in Parliament on Monday, Zelensky, his Polish and Baltic backers, and his army of internet supporters claimed that a Ukrainian strike on a Yandex data center in Russia the previous day had wiped thousands of “Russian bots” from social media.
As it turned out, none of this was true. The strike interrupted the activity of Yandex’ web crawler bots, which archive websites for search users, but with the help of an AI-created graph and some creative interpretation of the word “bot,” the hoax made it all the way to the Warsaw Security Forum.
French riots spread
French students took part in a fifth wave of demonstrations this week, which they say are aimed at securing more school funding and better learning conditions. Every wave of protests thus far has descended into rioting and vandalism, and this week’s marches were no different, with participants torching cars and battering police officers with cobblestones and fireworks in Paris.
RT’s Nadege Abderazzak watched heavily armored police baton-charge crowds of rioters in the French capital on Wednesday, noting that officers now outnumber protesters two-to-one at some rallies.
With French President Emmanuel Macron determined to increase military spending and continue arming Ukraine, France’s financial situation is in dire straits, and right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is on track to win the country’s next presidential election.
Meanwhile, Albanian students have taken a page out of their French counterparts’ book. After large protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha over corruption allegations, a crowd of students breached the fence of the Education Ministry in Tirana on Wednesday and torched the building.
Rama’s response has also drawn from the Western playbook, with the Albanian PM accusing protesters of waging “hybrid war” against the country.
What we’re watching
Zelensky may be in Trump’s bad books, but he can still count on the support of Macron, Burnham, and the rest of his European backers, whom he met in Brussels on Thursday and Friday. In his address to the European Council on Friday, the Ukrainian leader asked for another “70 billion euros” for ammunition, missiles, and air defense. Should Ukraine “fall,” Zelensky warned, another 20 million Ukrainian migrants will flood into the EU.
We’ll be keeping an eye on what kind of promises the cash-strapped Europeans make after this blatant shakedown.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will fly to Tehran on Monday for talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two diplomats are expected to focus on de-escalating the simmering US/Iran conflict in the Middle East, and any progress on this front will likely be reflected in global energy markets.
Lavrov will also meet Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic on Friday, ahead of critical parliamentary elections on October 25. Amid student protests, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic called the election early and stepped down to run as prime minister, a high-stakes move that turned the vote into a referendum on his nine years in power. With pro-Western students and right-wing ‘patriotic’ forces squeezing Vucic from either side, we’ll be keeping an eye out for polls, protests, and interference from the usual suspects.
For more on all of these stories, stick with RT.

articles.title: North Korea announced the testing of an AI-based torpedo system
articles.body:
North Korea announced the testing of an AI-based torpedo system
Kyiv • UNN
North Korea announced the testing of the Zam-2.0 torpedo system with artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance. Various tests were conducted 180 times over five years.
North Korea tested a "new-type" high-precision torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence to detect targets and guide itself, state media reported Saturday, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing. UNN reports this, citing AFP.
Details
The statement came days after Pyongyang said it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles, following weeks of tensions with Seoul over a mine explosion on their border.
North Korea tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles15.10.26, 07:50 • 5623 views
Analysts say North Korea may be rapidly developing its missile and weapons technologies with support from Russia, received in exchange for sending troops to support Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Underwater tests of the "superspeed" Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place Thursday "to confirm the successful technical upgrade" of the weapon, the Korean Central News Agency reported.
"Artificial intelligence technology was applied to the target detection and guidance functions of the new-type superspeed precision-guided torpedo," the Korean Central News Agency reported.
The test confirmed "the core technology for improving the efficiency of the propulsion system and the performance of the rocket engine," the report said, adding that "more than 180 rounds of various tests have been conducted over the past five years."
Earlier this month, North Korea announced the launch of an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
DPRK announces testing of latest missiles with AI27.05.26, 11:03 • 5596 views
Pyongyang then said there was "no way to avoid" the hypersonic missile, which is "capable of changing its flight trajectory at low altitude."
Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the claimed incorporation of artificial intelligence could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive maneuvers and make autonomous decisions to confuse adversaries, analysts say.
"South Korea and the United States deploy decoys to divert torpedoes, but artificial intelligence could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
"From torpedoes to submarine-based weapons, Pyongyang is devoting resources to demonstrating that U.S. strategic assets can be disabled," he said.
In September, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stressed the need to raise the "level of artificial intelligence" in the country’s weapons systems.

articles.title: North Korea says it tested AI-assisted precision-guided torpedo system
articles.body:
North Korea has tested a "new-type" precision-guided torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance, state media said, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing.
The announcement on Saturday came days after Pyongyang said it had test-fired two types of cruise missiles from a submarine after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border.
Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile and weapons technology with support from Russia received in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine.
The underwater test-fire of the "super-speed" Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place on Thursday "to confirm the successful technical updating" of the weapon, the Korean Central News Agency said.
"AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo," KCNA said.
The test proved "the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion device", it said, adding it had completed "more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years".
Earlier this month, North Korea announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Pyongyang said at the time there was "no way to avoid" the hypersonic missile, which was "capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude".
Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the stated introduction of AI could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive manoeuvres and make autonomous decisions to confuse an adversary, analysts say.
"South Korea and the United States deploy decoy targets to divert torpedoes, but AI could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University, told AFP news agency.
"From torpedoes to submarine-launched weapons, Pyongyang is pouring resources into demonstrating that US strategic assets can be rendered ineffective."
In September, Pyongyang's leader Kim Jong-un emphasised the need to raise "the level of artificial intelligence" in the country's weapons systems.
'Arms race'
Saturday's announcement came as the two Koreas appear to be intensifying an arms race over hypersonic missiles.
Hypersonic missiles travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can manoeuvre mid-flight, making them significantly harder to track and intercept.
Days after North Korea announced it had tested its AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile, Seoul test-fired its own weapon — a hypersonic glide vehicle it called a "key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield".
North Korea this week cast doubt on Seoul's test, saying it may have "failed to achieve hypersonic flight", a claim South Korea rejected a day later.
The latest weapons tests come amid growing speculation over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim, as world leaders prepare to gather for November's APEC summit in China.
After several overtures met with silence from Pyongyang, Trump said again this week he "may" meet North Korean leader Kim during his Asia tour next month.
Ahead of a possible North Korea-US summit, Pyongyang appears to be "playing down South Korea's hypersonic missile programme to portray itself as ahead of Seoul — Washington's ally — in the arms race", Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
But North Korea may need more time to advance its torpedo system, particularly in reducing the noise it generates underwater, he said.
"At high speeds underwater, a torpedo generates significant noise, making it easier to detect," Yang said.
"Reducing that noise is a major technical challenge requiring advanced technology — and North Korea does not yet appear to have reached that level."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
The Houthis continue to strike Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s threats of a forceful response and promises to enlist outside partners to defend the kingdom.
By targeting airports and oil infrastructure, Ansar Allah is seeking to raise the cost of Saudi involvement in Yemen’s conflict and force the kingdom’s leadership to reconsider the terms of a settlement.
The latest wave of Houthi attacks has targeted facilities of particular importance to Saudi Arabia. On the evening of October 13, a strike hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, home to the company’s key management operations. The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire, though miraculously no one was killed.
Ansar Allah also claimed strikes on an oil refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The choice of targets suggests the Houthis want to put virtually all of the kingdom’s oil revenue at risk and disrupt its international air connections.
These targets also suggest that the movement is trying to influence Saudi leaders’ decisions directly. Oil infrastructure generates government revenue, airports connect the country to the outside world, and confidence in the kingdom depends on the security of both. Even limited damage can therefore produce an impact far greater than the cost of the weapons used.
What is driving the conflict?
The Houthis have their own history of confrontation with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in northern Yemen, fought a series of wars against the central government between 2004 and 2010, and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Its rise was rooted in Yemen’s political system, local conflicts, and the collapse of state institutions. Iranian support strengthened an already established force with its own social base and political objectives.
The Saudi intervention in 2015 cemented Riyadh’s position as the movement’s principal foreign adversary. For the kingdom, the aim was to prevent a hostile force from consolidating power along its southern border and to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. For the Houthi leadership, the war became both a threat to its survival and a rallying cause. Invoking foreign aggression allowed the movement to portray its struggle for domestic supremacy as a defense of national sovereignty.
That logic remains relevant to the current escalation. Saudi support for an offensive by Yemeni government forces threatens the Houthis’ territorial gains and bargaining position. Striking deep inside the kingdom allows them to raise the price of that support. Their apparent calculation is to make continued Saudi involvement in the war carry a recurring cost on Saudi soil.
The movement’s demands are concrete: an end to strikes, limits on assistance to its Yemeni adversaries, the lifting of transportation and trade restrictions, and agreements on revenues and payments. These issues were under discussion long before the latest escalation. The framework for a roadmap presented by the UN in December 2023 included a nationwide ceasefire, payment of public-sector salaries, the resumption of oil exports, and an easing of restrictions on Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah.
By increasing Riyadh’s costs, Ansar Allah hopes to extract concessions and retain control of the territory it has seized. A ceasefire on those terms, however, would consolidate the movement’s position without resolving how power should be shared in Yemen.
Attacks on Saudi Arabia also serve Ansar Allah’s domestic political interests. The movement uses its ability to strike deep inside the kingdom to bolster its standing among supporters. Confrontation with Riyadh also allows the Houthis to cast themselves as Yemen’s defenders against foreign intervention and use that claim to justify their bid for power.
Iranian military and technological assistance has undoubtedly expanded Houthi capabilities considerably. But the relationship with Tehran does not erase Ansar Allah’s own interests in Yemen’s power struggle or its confrontation with Saudi Arabia. Reducing the movement’s actions to the execution of Iranian orders fails to explain either the conflict’s local roots or the Houthi leadership’s objectives.
A more accurate description would be a partnership with unequal resources in which the Yemeni side retains substantial autonomy. Weakening Saudi Arabia may serve both partners’ interests, but their preferred terms for ending the war may differ. Ansar Allah must consider conditions on Yemen’s battlefields and the survival of its own rule. Agreements between Iran and outside powers therefore do not guarantee an automatic halt to Houthi operations.
The economics of war
The development of domestic missile production and an expanding network for procuring components make it harder for Riyadh to bring Houthi attacks to an end. If the movement can replenish its arsenal from several sources, restricting Iranian supplies will have only a partial effect. An agreement with Tehran alone would therefore be insufficient to secure Saudi facilities. Much will depend on whether the Houthis themselves believe continued strikes serve their interests.
Nor do the Houthis need to match Saudi Arabia in the quantity or quality of their weapons. They can choose their targets and pause between attacks, while the kingdom must continuously defend airports, oil facilities, and cities across a vast territory. Even a single hit can disrupt a facility’s operations, trigger flight cancellations, or bring business activity to a halt. Purchases of American air defense systems reduce that threat but do not eliminate it. Riyadh’s problem is that military superiority has yet to deprive its adversary of the ability to inflict economically painful blows. That is precisely the capability the Houthis are trying to turn into negotiating leverage.
Saudi military spending exceeds $82 billion per year, yet the kingdom still struggles to protect its infrastructure from Houthi attacks. This exposes the gap between the cost of the weapons it has purchased and their effectiveness in this particular war. Advanced fighter jets and missile defense systems give Riyadh a considerable advantage, but detecting small drones and low-flying cruise missiles requires extensive radar coverage and rapid information sharing between units. Without those capabilities, expensive equipment cannot reliably detect and engage targets in time.
In a prolonged confrontation, the disparity in weapons costs also becomes significant. According to cited estimates, a Patriot interceptor costs more than $3 million, while some Houthi drones cost just $15,000–25,000. Defenders have to use such interceptors against cheap aircraft to protect far more valuable assets. But sustained defensive operations deplete stocks that cannot be replenished quickly, particularly amid strong global demand for air defense systems. This gives the Houthis an opportunity to wear down the kingdom’s defenses even when most of the aircraft they launch fail to reach their targets.
Technical difficulties are compounded by the structure of the Saudi armed forces. The separation of the regular military and the National Guard has historically served, in part, to protect the monarchy against a coup. But separate chains of command and highly centralized decision-making can hinder coordination and limit commanders’ initiative. Another weapons purchase, then, will not solve the problem on its own. Even additional detection and interception systems will deliver limited results if information arrives late and coordinating a response takes too long.
The Houthis can reasonably expect these shortcomings to take time to address, leaving them able to continue inflicting painful blows in the meantime. Domestic production and broader supply networks help sustain that campaign. The movement does not need to destroy major industrial facilities or shut down air travel altogether; a recurring threat is enough to make airlines reconsider routes, investors postpone decisions, and Saudi leaders spend more on protecting infrastructure.
Will help come from abroad?
Statements by Türkiye and Pakistan expressing their readiness to defend Saudi Arabia do not yet provide grounds to expect either country to enter the war fully, much less fight the Houthis inside Yemen. At an October 5 meeting, the parties to the Mecca Agreement announced that they would provide forces and equipment for the kingdom’s defense. The political weight of those promises, however, will depend on whether the allies can actually reduce the number of attacks and the damage they cause. As long as the strikes continue, Houthi leaders may view such declarations as rhetoric unlikely to be followed by a dangerous expansion of the war.
Ankara’s position reinforces that calculation. Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan outlined possible assistance with air defense, electronic warfare, and technical support, while explicitly ruling out Turkish troops taking part in offensive operations on foreign soil. Türkiye has thus set clear limits on its role from the outset.
Pakistan also has reasons to avoid direct intervention. Joining the war in Yemen would mean additional military spending and the risk of worsening relations with neighboring Iran. It would therefore be premature to expect Islamabad to take on the task of defeating the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf. Its commitments to the kingdom leave room for a role limited to defending specific facilities and providing military assistance.
A similar distinction applies to the American position. Intelligence sharing and targeting assistance support Saudi operations, but they do not mean Washington is willing to stop the attacks at any cost. The Houthis appear to be counting on precisely these limits to outside involvement. Their bet is that the kingdom’s allies will help it defend itself but will be reluctant to become embroiled in a prolonged war to achieve Saudi objectives in Yemen.
Until that support produces a substantial reduction in attacks, threats to bring in allies may carry little weight with Ansar Allah.
***
The Houthis are seeking to demonstrate that continued Saudi intervention will bring losses that neither a vast defense budget nor foreign partners can prevent. If that pressure prompts Riyadh to scale back assistance to their adversaries or accept settlement terms favorable to them, the movement will have an opportunity to translate its battlefield gains into lasting political advantages.
Such an outcome would also benefit Iran by weakening Saudi Arabia’s position. Its most immediate consequence, however, would be to strengthen Ansar Allah itself in the struggle for power in Yemen.

articles.title: Zelensky: ‘Putin’s Real Enemy Is the Rules-Based Order’ – Key Takeaways From Brussels
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned European leaders on Friday, Oct. 16, that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s real adversary is the rules-based international order, and urged the EU to stand together against Moscow’s aggression.
The Presidential Office published the full text of Zelensky’s address after he delivered it at the European Council meeting in Brussels. Zelensky spoke about Russia’s threat to Europe, Ukraine’s defense needs, sanctions, frozen Russian assets, Moldova and Kyiv’s path toward EU membership.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Putin’s target is Europe’s rules-based order
Zelensky said Putin’s “real enemy is an international order based on rules.” The Russian leader, he argued, is hostile to the EU not because of a specific policy or grievance, but because European unity and independent states stand in the way of a world in which leaders can wage war without consequences.
“If he wins, everything that holds you together and keeps your people living in peace will simply be gone,” Zelensky said. He pointed to Putin’s criticism of developments since 1985, saying: “We don’t want to go back there.”
Zelensky also recalled Russia’s war against Chechnya. He said it taught Putin that oil and gas could be used to “tempt the world” and persuade politicians to look away even as cities were destroyed. He urged the EU not to ease sanctions, warning that Russia uses every opportunity to restore revenues and fund its war.
Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
Ukraine asks Europe for €70 billion and air defense
Zelensky said the war would cost Ukraine €155 billion in 2027 and asked European partners for at least €70 billion more for defense, weapons and resilience. He said Ukraine could produce two or three times more drones, depending on the type, if it had enough funding.
He also urged EU countries to provide 300 Patriot interceptors to help defend Ukraine against ballistic missiles and called for a strong 22nd EU sanctions package targeting people and companies involved in Russia’s missile, communications and drone industries.
Zelensky asked Europe to protect frozen Russian assets so they could be used to support Ukraine. He warned that if the EU failed to act, Putin could find a way to regain control of the money and use it to finance the war.
Zelensky links Ukraine’s defense to Europe’s security
Zelensky said Ukraine’s army and military technologies help protect Europe, arguing that the continent’s security guarantees cannot be built without Ukraine’s experience and defense capabilities. He warned that Putin was building a Russia resembling North Korea, where children are raised from an early age for war and to die for their leader.
The president also said Ukraine was helping Moldova counter Russian efforts to destabilize the country through Transnistria. According to Zelensky, this requires work by Ukraine’s security and intelligence services, as well as moving some military forces away from other tasks to keep risks under control.
He argued that separating Ukraine and Moldova on their path toward EU membership would be morally wrong. Ukraine, he said, is helping Moldova remain stable and independent, and the two countries should move forward together. Four EU accession clusters have opened for Ukraine this year, Zelensky said, with two more remaining. Kyiv Post previously reported on the accession-cluster process.
Zelensky ended by reiterating Ukraine’s European aspirations, saying the country would join the EU and that more people recognize its importance to NATO. He urged European leaders to account for Ukraine’s defense role in the bloc’s long-term budget and keep working together to strengthen European security.

articles.title: What if NATO’s ‘Theory of Victory’ is a recipe for disaster?
articles.body:
What if NATO’s ‘Theory of Victory’ is a recipe for disaster?
On October 5, 2026, at the Warsaw Security Forum, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Alexus Grynkewich unveiled a military strategy titled ‘Theory of Victory’.
The strategy covers the next few years and outlines NATO’s preparations to counter a potential “Russian attack.” While the details are likely classified, the main points have been made public. Here are the key publicly disclosed aspects of NATO’s ‘victory’ plan:
- Economic exhaustion of the adversary: The development of military and industrial capabilities that would make continued hostilities costly and futile for the aggressor. Here, NATO is positioning itself as the defending party.
- Destruction of support infrastructure: Strikes against the enemy’s infrastructure, targeting not only the attacking forces but also the entire system sustaining the armed forces – logistics, command centers, supply lines, and reserves.
- 2029 as the operational readiness benchmark: By 2029, the US Armed Forces and NATO’s European allies must complete the main preparations for countering potential global threats and must be ready to address any external challenge.
- NATO’s technological superiority: This point emphasizes achieving comprehensive technological dominance through the widespread use of drones and AI-driven combat management systems.
That’s the ‘theory of victory’; now, it has to be put into practice. Certain types of political documents don’t present any interest as long as they’re stored in bureaucratic folders – no one cares about numbers, timelines, logistics, and readiness levels. But once they enter the public domain, they quickly acquire symbolic meaning. A “defense plan” becomes a “war plan,” “deterrence” turns into “targeting,” and a simple date on a calendar becomes a prophecy. This is precisely the case with this strategy. Formally, NATO’s plan doesn’t contain anything sensational: it talks about strengthening the eastern flank, preparing equipment and resources, expanding exercises, aligning industrial capabilities with evolving needs, setting readiness targets, integrating air and missile defense systems, creating logistical routes, and developing crisis response scenarios. All of this has been part of NATO’s alarmist yet necessary routine for decades. However, this time, something new has been added: a deadline!
And the deadline – 2029 – resonates not just as an administrative milestone but as a psychological turning point.
The question that comes to mind is both simple and unsettling: how dangerous is it to prepare society, the military, and politics for a threat that may be driven by fear rather than grounded in reality? ‘Being prepared’ is one thing; but can it lead to the idea that ‘since we’re prepared, we can be the first to act’? 
Let’s talk about the potential threat. The rhetoric, plans, and timelines all point to a specific year: 2030. Various Western ‘seers’ suggest that this is when ‘Eastern hordes’ will charge westward. In other words, Western analysts anticipate a Russian assault on NATO countries around this time. At the same time, NATO leadership candidly states that currently, the threat from Russia is assessed as minimal. But by 2030, Russia will be ready!
It’s tempting to call this the “mythical Russian threat,” but the term “mythical” has been used so often that it has lost its meaning. It seems to create a divide between those who “believe in the threat” and those who “perceive reality.” However, geopolitics rarely fits neatly into black-and-white categories. A threat can be simultaneously real, exaggerated, distorted, and dangerous, precisely because it contains a kernel of truth.
In reality, Russia doesn’t even have the personnel and resources to attack NATO – unless one assumes such an attack would be suicidal in nature. Nevertheless, the existence of an external enemy provides excellent justification for any political initiatives, and this concept seems to have been embraced by NATO as the primary driver for development.
According to NATO’s charter, it is strictly a defensive alliance. Article 5 discusses collective defense, not preemptive strikes. Regional plans, exercises, troop movements, and forward basing are designed as deterrents: to demonstrate to potential adversaries that aggression would come at too great a cost. However, active preparation for defense and the resulting substantial military buildup could offer politicians new options that might tempt them to act.
Finally, measures that one state views as protective can be perceived by another as a threat to its security. This sets off a spiral of escalation and mutual intimidation, pushing both sides into a standoff where they’re heavily armed for ‘deterrence’ yet unable to pass each other without starting a conflict. Although NATO’s plans may appear defensive on paper, they trigger this very mechanism – especially when accompanied by public rhetoric like “Russia could attack in a few years,” “Europe must be prepared by 2030,” or “the window of opportunity is closing.” While these statements may reflect genuine concerns, they also create a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Of course, in defense planning, timelines are essential. Without them, the military risks becoming a bureaucratic museum, while the defense industry could turn into a shop selling antique rifles. However, deadlines have a downside; they turn preparedness into a race. In public discourse, 2029 begins to sound less like a guideline and more like a deadline. By 2029, forces, equipment, munitions, logistical routes, command structures, trained reserves, integrated air defense systems, intelligence networks, and industrial capacities should be in place. This goal is quite reasonable for a military document.
But it raises a key question: what happens if someone in NATO eventually says, “We’re ready!”? This may first emerge as a report or assessment and may then be proclaimed as a political achievement; next, it may be used as an argument, and in times of crisis it may very well become a temptation to act.
The logic of preemptive action always appeals to those who fear they might miss the boat. ‘If we wait, our adversary will grow stronger. If we strike now, we can avert a major war’ – this reasoning is as old as time and often deeply manipulative; it appears rational until it leads to death and destruction.
Preemptive “threat prevention” is an oxymoron. According to this logic, to prevent a war, one must start a war; to avoid a strike, one must strike first; to protect the status quo, one must disrupt it. Most importantly, no one can guarantee that retaliation will be limited, that escalation will stop at the desired threshold, that nuclear weapons will not be used, that allies will remain loyal, or that the public will bear the costs of the war.
The temptation exists. But can we halt escalation before it spirals into a full-blown crisis? There may still be a chance.
Firstly, transparency is crucial. We’re not talking about the disclosure of combat plans, but about clear signals regarding the kinds of actions that are considered defensive; limitations on certain military exercises; the types of forces that are not intended for a first strike; and the types of communication channels that will remain open even during crises.
Secondly, rules for de-escalation are necessary. These could include notifications about military activities, major exercises, limitations on movements near borders, incident verification mechanisms, military hotlines, and agreements on the actions of drones, aircraft, and vessels in contested areas.
Thirdly, political leaders must consistently distinguish readiness from resolve. There is a difference between being prepared to defend oneself and launching a preemptive strike. This distinction needs to be emphasized not just in official documents but also in public statements.
Fourthly, we need responsible journalism and analytical insight. What’s required is neither naive reassurance – claiming there’s no threat – nor panic-driven claims that war is imminent. The goal should be to reflect the complexity of the world. A threat can be considered significant, but it may not necessitate war; and deterrence can be firm without leading to aggression.
And lastly, we must work to restore at least minimal arms control frameworks. Without them, each side will feel compelled to run faster, even if the race leads both to jump off a cliff.
The year 2029 could be when Europe becomes stronger and more resilient. Or, it might be the year when someone declares, ‘We’re ready, and we can do anything!’ The former concept is about deterrence; the latter is deterrence in its perverted form. It’s crucial for all parties in this race to understand this clearly.

articles.title: Russia Prepares Western Strikes Via Belarus
articles.body:
Russian forces are preparing to intensify strikes against western Ukrainian regions, increasingly drawing Belarus into the war by installing drone signal repeaters and seeking to deploy ballistic missile batteries on Belarusian territory, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Zelensky explained that Moscow is already utilizing Belarusian soil to establish drone transit corridors into western Ukraine and is actively pressing Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko for permission to base advanced ballistic missile systems within the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This is not enough for them. They need Lukashenko’s support so that other weapon types, including ballistics, are based on the territory of Belarus,” Zelensky said.
“Undoubtedly, the deployment of ballistics in Belarus will pose a threat primarily to the western part of our state.”
The Ukrainian head of state stressed that the risk of expanding aerial strikes targeting western provinces is acute and that Russian President Vladimir Putin possesses concrete operational blueprints to initiate such attacks, cautioning that deploying ballistic launchers from Belarus would represent Minsk’s direct military entry into active hostilities.
Targeting of ports, water utilities, and bridges
Zelensky observed that the Kremlin’s strategic targeting parameters remain fixed on systematically destroying Ukrainian life-support networks and maritime commerce ahead of the winter heating season.
Zelensky: Starlink Capped at 161 km/h, Disabling Interceptors
According to the president, Russian forces continue to prioritize strikes against electricity networks, municipal water distribution systems, civilian river bridges, and commercial port infrastructure across the Black Sea littoral.
“They have struck, are striking, and will continue to strike and blockade port infrastructure in the Black Sea,” Zelensky told reporters. “Unfortunately, they have struck and are striking our energy and everything connected to water supply.”
Zelensky highlighted that key transit bridges remain regular targets of Russian loitering munitions and cruise missiles, noting that while Ukrainian air defenses intercept the majority of incoming threats, munitions periodically penetrate protective envelopes.
“We shoot down everything we can, but we also see what gets through,” Zelensky said. “We need to respond to their strikes. If we show weakness, nothing will stop him. He will demand capitulation, although even that will not be enough for him.”
The president reiterated that deterrence and reciprocal pressure remain the only viable mechanisms to halt Russian escalation and compel Moscow to accept an enforceable ceasefire.
Drone signal repeaters and Minsk’s ‘co-aggressor’ role
The deployment of radio and cellular signal repeaters across southern Belarus allows Russian military operators to maintain stable command-and-control links with long-range strike drones navigating at low altitudes, effectively transforming Belarusian airspace into a staging vector to strike western Ukrainian logistics corridors.
The warning unfolds against a backdrop of deep strategic integration between Moscow and Minsk. On Oct. 2, Lukashenko openly described himself and Putin as “co-aggressors” during a meeting of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, affirming that Belarus remains unconditionally aligned with the Kremlin’s military campaign.
“In the end, we are ‘co-aggressors’ with him. We have one question, which we sometimes discuss jokingly: who is more of an ‘aggressor’ – me or him?” Lukashenko stated at the time, pledging that Belarusian authorities would back any strategic decision made by Moscow.

“We Will Strike Strategic Bridges”: Russia Threatens to Split Kyiv in Two
Russian military forces intend to split Kyiv in two by carrying out strikes on strategic bridges across Ukraine, according to statements by Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov.
The announcement came as Moscow initiated massive strikes against the country's energy infrastructure, while official Kremlin statements explicitly ruled out discussing border safety zones in future negotiations, according to 24tv.

Officials addressed several operational metrics and military objectives. Kremlin representatives stated that around 10% of the Donetsk region and roughly 16.5% of the Zaporizhzhia region remain under Ukrainian control.
Valery Gerasimov reported that since September 1, Russian forces captured over 1,800 square kilometers of territory and 92 settlements, while claiming that a 2,000-strong Ukrainian group was destroyed in the northeastern Kharkiv region.

Addressing air defense and overall strategy, Vladimir Putin stated that “Russia needs to increase the effectiveness of air defense” and directed that “launching massive and group strikes against Ukrainian facilities must be continued.” Meanwhile, Valery Gerasimov announced: “We will strike strategic bridges in Ukraine.”
On October 14, 2026, Russia launched a massive overnight attack against Ukrainian infrastructure, firing 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones at Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. Ukrainian air defenses neutralized 115 UAVs and four ballistic missiles, but the strikes damaged 26 power grid facilities and four oil and gas sites, leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity.
Monitoring channels reported that a record barrage of roughly 25 Zircon hypersonic missiles targeted the capital and surrounding areas. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the assault as a deliberate strike on energy infrastructure previously covered by a ceasefire, calling the scale of the operation an open display of disrespect toward the United States.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill 7, injure dozens across Ukraine amid continued strikes on energy infrastructure
articles.body:
Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid as US 'disregards' Graham's sanctions, Zelensky says
Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russian attacks against Ukraine killed seven people and injured around 90 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 17, with the country reporting one of the heaviest Russian attacks against energy infrastructure so far.
Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported. Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas, according to the statement.
The attacks came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter. Attacks on energy facilities across the country overnight and on the morning of Oct. 17 left some homes without power, the Energy Ministry said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky described Russia's latest attack as "one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure." Russian forces targeted more than 15 key power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine, he said.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky said on social media, calling on Washington to pressure Moscow through a "sanctions blackout."
"Financial rewards for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground."
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed a man and a woman, aged 58 and 71. Another 41 people were injured or suffered from stress, including three children, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Four women and three men were injured in Sumy Oblast in Russian drone attacks, local authorities reported.
Russian attacks near the city of Nikopol in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed a 74-year-old woman and injured two men over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. One more man was killed in Dnipro, the regional center, after Russian forces targeted an industrial facility.
Russia launched one of its largest attacks on central Vinnytsia Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion, targeting civilian and critical infrastructure with drones and injuring six people, Governor Natalia Zabolotna said.
Russian forces targeted civilian infrastructure in Odesa Oblast, injuring at least four people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Fifteen more people were injured in the region over the past day.
Russian troops also attacked Zaporizhzhia Oblast, injuring six people, said Ivan Fedorov, head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces targeted 31 towns and villages, including the regional center of Kherson. One person was killed, and at least 19 others were injured, including children, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported.

articles.title: Russian Overnight Attack Kills Civilians, Targets Energy Facilities Across Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia struck Ukraine overnight with ballistic and cruise missiles as well as hundreds of drones, killing civilians and damaging residential buildings, Ukrainian authorities said on October 17.
The attacks also disrupted power supply in several regions, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the barrage "one of [Russia's] largest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector," adding that more than 15 "critical power generation and transmission facilities" were targeted across the country.
Writing on X on October 17, he said the worst-hit areas included Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsya, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn, and that "energy facilities in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Dnipro, and other regions were also hit."
"The Russians have scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to stretch our reserves and repair capabilities as thin as possible," Zelenskyy wrote.
"Between 7 p.m. yesterday and 7 a.m. today alone, more than 320 jet-powered and gasoline-powered 'shaheds,' along with loitering munitions, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, were used against our energy sector, our cities, and our communities."
Russia launched four Kalibr cruise missiles and 332 attack drones, including 31 jet-powered drones, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles and Kh-22/32 cruise missiles, according to Ukraine's air force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 293 aerial targets, including all four Kalibr missiles and 289 drones, the air force said. Impacts were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at three others.
In the southern city of Kherson, a Russian air strike on the Korabelniy district killed a 64-year-old emergency medical services driver, regional military administration head Yaroslav Shanko said.
In Slovyansk, in the eastern Donetsk region, Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood with FAB-250 aerial bombs in the early hours of the morning, hitting two apartment buildings, according to local authorities.
One person was killed and 10 others were wounded in the attack, four of whom were hospitalized. Search-and-rescue operations were under way, with people potentially trapped beneath the rubble of both buildings.
Eight apartment buildings were damaged, two of them partially destroyed. A total of 16 people were wounded in Slovyansk over the past 24 hours, including a 17-year-old girl. Vehicles and municipal equipment were also damaged.
The strikes also placed further strain on Ukraine's electricity system. National grid operator Ukrenergo announced emergency power cuts in several regions, saying previously published outage schedules would not apply in areas affected by the measures.
Energy workers were working to restore supplies, and authorities urged consumers who still had electricity to use it sparingly.
In Vinnytsya, the regional capital in central Ukraine, Russian attacks left the city without electricity, Mayor Serhiy Morhunov said. Officials were assessing the extent of the damage, while critical infrastructure switched to backup power.
The latest barrage came as US President Donald Trump announced that he had waived nearly all substantive sanctions, tariffs, and restrictions included in a bipartisan law aimed at pressuring Russia to end its war against Ukraine.
The move prompted sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff said on October 17 that Ukrainian forces remained in control of the eastern town of Dobropillia in Donetsk region, rejecting a claim by Russian President Vladimir Putin a day earlier that Russian forces had captured the town.
Kyiv also disputed Moscow's claim that Russian forces had seized more than 1,800 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 92 settlements since September 1, Reuters reported.
Among other hard-line demands for ending its long-running invasion, Russia has repeatedly said Ukraine must hand over the part of the eastern Donetsk region that Moscow's forces have been unable to capture despite years of deadly fighting.
Ukraine says this is unacceptable, signaling it could agree to a cease-fire that would leave the front lines in place as talks get under way.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Russian Drone Interceptions and Food Deliveries to Frontline Troops
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, Oct. 16, that Ukraine’s military Starlink satellite communications capabilities have still not been fully restored, warning that restrictions on the US-provided system had prevented Ukrainian forces from shooting down Russian jet-powered drones and disrupted essential supplies to frontline soldiers.
Speaking at a press conference in Brussels after meeting EU leaders, Zelensky said the restrictions were gradually being reversed but that Ukraine had not regained the full operating capabilities needed to protect civilians against Russia’s increasingly fast attack drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes,” Zelensky said.
The president’s comments came as a Reuters investigation raised fresh questions about Washington’s role in restrictions affecting Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield network, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Zelensky said Ukraine’s Defense Ministry remained in daily contact with partners to resolve the disruption and restore the capabilities Ukrainian forces previously possessed.
He revealed that he had received information suggesting the White House had contacted SpaceX about reversing the restrictions.
“Our partners told me there was a signal from the White House administration to SpaceX to restore this,” Zelensky said.
Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing US National Interest
“I don’t know whether that’s true or not. If it is, we are very grateful.”
Despite the reported intervention, the Zelensky made clear that the problem had not been fully resolved.
Russian Shaheds outpace restricted Ukrainian interceptors
Zelensky offered a detailed explanation of how Starlink restrictions undermined Ukraine’s defense against jet-powered Shahed drones, which Russia has increasingly deployed against Ukrainian cities.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that come and strike our civilians and kill our families,” he said.
“We use special interceptors that move at very high speeds – interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink.”
According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s satellite terminals were subjected to restrictions that prevented high-speed drones from maintaining the connections required for their missions.
“Starlink was not switched off. The speed was reduced,” he said.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down some of the Shaheds.”
Zelensky said Russian jet-powered drones were flying at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (249 mph), while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems had faced a movement-speed threshold of approximately 70 km/h (43 mph).
The consequences, Zelensky said, were particularly serious because the affected drones were intended to stop Russian attacks before they reached civilian areas.
“We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians,” he said.
“This is very painful and unpleasant.”
Starlink restrictions disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian troops
Zelensky said the Starlink restrictions also disrupted food and water deliveries to Ukrainian soldiers holding frontline positions under constant Russian drone surveillance, where conventional supply vehicles cannot safely reach them.
“Our most important thing is people,” Zelensky said.
“Food and water are delivered to our soldiers, who spend weeks and months on the front line, using drones equipped with Starlink,” he said.
Those operations require drones capable of traveling at high speeds, making satellite communication restrictions particularly disruptive.
Zelensky said the limitations interfered with these deliveries while simultaneously weakening Ukraine’s ability to intercept drones targeting civilians.
“They were cutting off our logistics and the protection of the civilian population,” he said.
Ukraine seeks independence from US-controlled military technology
Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine continues to rely on US intelligence for early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches, despite receiving intelligence from dozens of other countries.
“Regarding ballistic missiles, specifically information about their launches, we receive that information from the United States,” he explained.
“As you can see, there are many challenges, particularly those related to ballistic missiles.”
Zelensky said Ukraine was working to reduce such vulnerabilities by strengthening its own technological capabilities and cooperation with European partners.
“We are working on every possible option to make Ukraine as independent as possible,” he said.

articles.title: Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Russian forces launched one of their largest coordinated assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, striking more than 15 critical electricity generation and transmission facilities across multiple provinces, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
The president reported that emergency restoration operations are underway across the country, mobilizing municipal utility workers and specialized engineering crews from domestic power companies to restore severed power supplies.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“On the eve, the Russians delivered one of their largest strikes against Ukrainian energy: more than 15 critical electricity generation and energy transmission facilities in various regions of Ukraine were attacked,” Zelensky stated.
“Restoration work is ongoing, involving all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies. I thank everyone working virtually non-stop to restore power.”
Regional impact and grid dispersion tactics
Zelensky highlighted that the most severe disruptions to municipal electricity networks were recorded in northwestern and central urban centers, specifically identifying Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn.
Additional kinetic strikes and falling debris damaged energy installations across Kharkiv region, Kyiv region, and Dnipropetrovsk region alongside other administrative jurisdictions.
According to the president, the operational breadth of the assault reflects an intentional Russian doctrine engineered to exhaust municipal repair reserves and disperse domestic technical response teams ahead of freezing winter temperatures.
EU Tasks Commission to Bridge Ukraine’s €70B Funding Gap
“The Russians scaled up their anti-energy operation and are trying to disperse our reserves and recovery capacity to the maximum,” Zelensky said.
Between 7:00 p.m. on Friday and 7:00 a.m. on Saturday, Russian forces deployed more than 320 strike drones against Ukraine’s civil power networks, municipal infrastructure, and residential settlements.
The wave comprised a mix of turbojet-powered and conventional piston-engine Shahed loitering munitions, loitering compact cruise weapons, alongside cruise and ballistic missiles.
“And although our warriors manage to shoot down a significant portion, the scale and continuity of Russian strikes – specifically against energy – unfortunately has many negative consequences,” Zelensky noted.
Push for European support
Zelensky confirmed that European partner nations have assembled new military and energy assistance packages to reinforce Ukrainian defenses, expressing gratitude for European solidarity following high-level summits in Brussels.
Concurrently, the president addressed policymakers and the public in the US, criticizing recent decisions in Washington to waive statutory economic sanctions and tariffs targeting the Russia.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is actually happening,” Zelensky emphasized.
“At a time when the Russians delivered such a massive strike against our energy, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war.”
The presidential statement referred to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which US President Donald Trump signed into law on Sept. 18 but waived via executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, just 48 hours before mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum buyers were set to take effect.
“This law could – and still can! – help greatly. But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for this matters,” Zelensky urged, noting that relieving economic pressure incentivizes further aggression.
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating,” Zelensky stated.
“Pressure is needed to stop this. An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to strike further. We must not surrender positions; we must try to end the war. End it, rather than give Putin every reason to prolong it indefinitely.”
