articles.title: Trump feud with Zelenskyy raises fears over Ukraine aid
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s growing dispute with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is raising concerns that Kyiv could lose critical American military and intelligence support as Russia continues its war, with Washington’s efforts to curb fuel prices adding to tensions between the allies.
From threats to restrict intelligence sharing to a potential deal to import Russian diesel, a series of developments has exposed the fragility of the relationship between Kyiv and its most important ally.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelenskyy over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he partly blames for rising energy costs.
The U.S. president has pushed Ukraine to stop targeting Russian energy infrastructure, but Zelenskyy has rejected the demand, arguing that Kyiv cannot halt its attacks while Moscow continues striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The dispute intensified after disruptions to U.S.-controlled satellite internet services raised concerns about Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly as it prepares for another winter of assaults on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy has responded to Trump with unusually direct public criticism, accusing Washington of increasingly favoring Moscow.
His remarks have fueled fears that the deteriorating relationship could lead to further restrictions on U.S. weapons deliveries, a suspension of battlefield intelligence sharing or additional economic agreements that benefit Russia.
Despite the public confrontation, Kyiv wants to maintain contact with Trump's envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Ukraine is also seeking to preserve its diplomatic relationship with Washington.
Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said Friday that Kyiv appreciated Trump's efforts to end the war and remained willing to engage in negotiations with Russia.
Trump, meanwhile, said he would continue dealing with both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I want that war to end," Trump told reporters Friday.
Daniel Fried, a former senior State Department official responsible for European affairs from 2005 to 2009, said it remained unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine.
He warned, however, that the fallout was undermining prospects for ending the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy has been strained for much of his presidency. In February 2025, Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly reprimanded the Ukrainian leader during a contentious meeting in the Oval Office.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine at various points, while allowing European allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
Relations had shown signs of stabilizing before Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities became a fresh source of friction this year.
Rising fuel prices have added urgency to the dispute for Trump, whose Republican Party faces a difficult battle to retain its majorities in Congress in November's midterm elections. High gasoline and diesel costs remain a political liability for the administration, analysts say.
But experts attribute much of the increase in energy prices to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which prompted Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure and largely shut the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated with Zelenskyy, Trump turned to Moscow in an effort to increase fuel supplies and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Trump said Oct. 9 that he had reached an agreement with Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
The move raised concerns that Washington could ease economic pressure on Moscow while demanding concessions from Ukraine, potentially giving the Kremlin additional revenue to sustain its war effort.
For Kyiv, the consequences of a breakdown in relations with Washington could be immediate.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital, underscoring concerns about the reliability of intelligence support.
American intelligence has been central to Ukraine's ability to detect incoming Russian missiles and drones, assess battlefield developments and plan military operations. A reduction in that assistance could leave Ukrainian forces less prepared to counter attacks, particularly against power plants and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy system during previous winters, seeking to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall.
Trump has said Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv. Zelenskyy, however, told NPR that U.S. officials had warned Ukrainian commanders that intelligence support could be reduced or cut off.
Concerns deepened after Ukraine's Starshield service, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system, was disrupted. Two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said the disruption followed an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported Thursday.
The service has since been partially restored, but the episode highlighted Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by American companies and potentially affected by decisions made by the Trump administration.
Satellite communications are crucial to Ukrainian military coordination, particularly on the front lines. Any prolonged interruption could complicate communications between units and undermine operational effectiveness.
That dependence also gives Trump leverage as he presses Kyiv to pursue negotiations with Moscow.
Trump's approach could face resistance from Republicans in Congress who remain supportive of Ukraine and oppose pressuring Kyiv into a settlement that favors Russia.
Some lawmakers have argued that Washington should maintain support for Ukraine rather than allow Moscow to benefit from a weakening of Western assistance.
Zelenskyy's increasingly forceful responses to Trump carry risks, particularly given Washington's influence over Ukraine's military capabilities. But he may be betting that the balance of power in Congress could shift after the November midterm elections, making it more difficult for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or further reduce assistance to Kyiv.
That is the assessment of Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration who heads the Global Situation Room consultancy.
Bruen said Zelenskyy understood the risks of confronting Trump but appeared less intimidated by the president's threats than during earlier clashes.
"Zelenskyy knows who he's dealing with," he said. "Trump's threats don't have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office."

articles.title: Belgium Confirms Delivery of 10 F-16 Fighter Jets to Ukraine by End of 2026
articles.body:

Belgium Confirms Delivery of 10 F-16 Fighter Jets to Ukraine by End of 2026
As Russia increasingly deploys faster jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine, Belgium is preparing to strengthen Kyiv’s air defenses with additional F-16 fighter jets, whose 20mm cannons could provide a new advantage in intercepting aerial threats.
Belgium has confirmed plans to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, despite earlier delays caused by the slower-than-expected arrival of US-made F-35 fighters intended to replace its existing fleet.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Brussels Times on October 16, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever confirmed the timeline following talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels.
De Wever explained that Belgium’s ability to transfer the aircraft depends on receiving new F-35 fighters, which are gradually replacing the country’s aging F-16 fleet.
The deliveries have fallen behind schedule because of delays in the F-35 program. However, with replacement aircraft now arriving, Belgium expects to proceed with the transfers while maintaining its commitments to NATO.
The Belgian prime minister emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs additional combat aircraft, particularly to counter Russia’s growing use of jet-powered attack drones.
He identified the F-16's 20mm cannon as a potentially effective weapon against these threats, allowing Ukrainian pilots to engage incoming drones without relying exclusively on air-to-air missiles.
Beyond intercepting Russian drones, the aircraft could strengthen Ukraine’s ability to protect its cities, energy infrastructure, and Black Sea grain export routes.
During their meeting, De Wever and Zelenskyy also discussed accelerating military assistance and supplying additional ammunition for the aircraft.
Belgian defense manufacturer FN Herstal produces 20mm ammunition compatible with the F-16's cannon, making the country a potential supplier of munitions needed for Ukraine’s air defense operations.
De Wever did not specify whether all 10 aircraft in the revised delivery plan would be combat-ready or whether some would be designated for maintenance and spare parts.
Belgium initially committed in May 2024 to supplying Ukraine with 30 F-16 fighters by 2028. The delivery schedule subsequently faced setbacks as the Belgian Air Component awaited replacement F-35 aircraft.
Ukraine’s combined fleet of Western-made F-16 and Mirage 2000 fighter jets now outnumbers its remaining Soviet-era MiG-29s and Su-27s. F-16s are playing an increasingly important role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones as Ukraine expands its Western fighter fleet and strengthens its air defenses.

articles.title: Ukraine strengthens air defence in west, views deployment of ballistic missiles in Belarus as attempt to draw it into war – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is convinced that Russia is preparing to intensify its attacks on western Ukraine and is attempting to use Belarus to that end.
"I think so," Zelenskyy said on Saturday, responding to journalists' questions about whether there is a threat of increased attacks on western Ukraine and whether Russia is preparing for this.
"Why, in my view, are they constantly dragging Belarus into this? Because we know that they are placing relay stations on Belarusian territory to use this corridor for drones and to intensify such attacks. But that's not enough for them: they need Lukashenko's support so that other types of weapons, including ballistic missiles, can be deployed on Belarusian territory," the Ukrainian president added.
He said he would regard the deployment of Russian ballistic weapons in Belarus as a direct involvement of Belarus in the war against Ukraine. "Undoubtedly, the deployment of ballistic missiles on Belarusian territory poses a threat first and foremost to the western part of our country. I am confident that Putin shares this view. But this is a direct involvement of Belarus in this war, and it is, in my view, very dangerous. And, of course, for Belarus as well. And God forbid that they get dragged into this," Zelenskyy said.
He also announced the strengthening of air defense in the relevant regions. "We're strengthening our defenses based on the principle that where there are more strikes, there will be more air defense. And, of course, it's very important for us to increase air defense capabilities throughout our country… Where there's a greater threat, there will be greater protection," Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia reports incoming fire as Egypt weighs sending help
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia said on Saturday that it had intercepted a fresh wave of incoming drones, as its ally Egypt weighed sending the kingdom help in defending against repeated attacks from Yemen's Houthis.
Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis, and media affiliated with the Iran-backed group reported on Saturday that Saudi airstrikes beginning overnight had killed at least 12 people.
Since Yemen's conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh's airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Saturday that it had "intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South".
The interceptions came as the president of Egypt, which is also a member of the coalition, said he was willing to "carry out any measure to protect" Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was "harmed or its security and stability threatened".
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," he said. "We are speaking only about defence."
French mayor: Attack shows Israel 'tolerance' for violence
A French mayor who was attacked Saturday by Israeli settlers in the West Bank told AFP that the incident showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, said after he was attacked on a goodwill visit to the town of Taybeh.
West Bank settlers attack Palestinians, Western diplomats
Masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives and Western diplomats and officials, Belgium's foreign minister said on Saturday.
Maxime Prevot said the Belgian consul general, French and Polish diplomats and a French mayor were among those attacked, while a Belgian vehicle was damaged.
"Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," Prevot said.
Belgium will continue to press for sanctions against those responsible for the violence and those who support them, Prevot said.
The Israeli military, the European Commission and French and Polish foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested", as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
Since Yemen's war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added that it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened".
"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said.
He added that any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorisation "if it is requested of us".
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defence."
Saudi strikes that began overnight have killed at least 12 people in Yemen, three of them children, Houthi media reported on Saturday.
Saudi warplanes targeted "civilian homes" in Taiz governorate on Saturday, killing nine people and wounding 16, the Iran-backed group's news agency said, adding that people were still trapped under the rubble.
The agency had earlier reported overnight strikes in Dhamar province that killed three children and wounded 17 other people.
It said the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally".
Saudi Arabia said on Saturday that it had intercepted four drones, including over the capital Riyadh, as the country comes under repeated fire from Yemen's Houthis.
"We have intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in the regions of Riyadh, the Eastern Province, and the South," Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed group, wrote on X.
UKMTO reports incident 140 nautical miles in al Mukalla
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Saturday that it had received a report of an incident 140 nautical miles (259 km) southeast of Yemen's Al Mukalla.
The captain of an LNG tanker reported that a small skiff carrying seven people approached the vessel and fired two shots at it, UKMTO said in an advisory note.
The tanker's armed security team fired two warning shots at the skiff, forcing it to alter course, it added.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Saturday that the IMF intends to support Iraq "very firmly" with a requested loan program, while there were "intense" discussions on support for Lebanon reflecting significant progress towards a loan program.
"We will get to Iraq both money and policy support. In the case of Lebanon, we are in very intense discussions with the Lebanese authorities," Georgieva told a closing news conference at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
"We have made significant progress towards the program. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I'm confident we will be successful."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Putin is looking to cause Ukraine-wide ‘blackout’
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy waits for Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson ahead of their bilateral meeting on the sidelines of a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels on October 16, 2026. | Olivier Hoslet/ AFP via Getty Images
Starlink restrictions hampering Ukraine’s war effort are “a planned operation,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
The satellite service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX is still deactivated in Ukraine at speeds over 160 km/h, which prevents some of its drones to intercept high-speed Shahed drones used by Russia, Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat.
He added that Ukraine conducted a test by sending Starlink-equipped vehicules to European Union countries, at speeds over 180 km/h. “Starlink kept working … The conclusion is this: the restrictions are in effect in Ukraine, but they are not in effect in European Union countries. So, this is a planned operation,” Zelenskyy said.
Advertisement
The restrictions have revived questions on Ukraine’s reliance on the satellite system operated by a U.S. company amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the White House. “This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network earlier this week.
“We’re reaching out to everyone at the military level, at the Ministry of Defense level, and at the diplomatic level, including to SpaceX. Right now, no one is responding to our military or the Ministry of Defense,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
The European Union is under increasing pressure to provide Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink. But negotiations between Brussels and Kyiv over access to the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities— have been stalling. And IRIS², the EU’s in-house planned network to match Starlink, is only expected to come online in 2030.
“The Europeans are now raising the question of alternatives themselves. And they’re already working on them. They’re already making progress, and they’ll succeed in this area. I can already see that,” Zelenskyy said.
SpaceX did not immediately responded to a request for comment.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy accused Russia of looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.
Advertisement
“Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said on Telegram.
“An American sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, monetary rewards for [Russian President Vladimir] Putin: all of this only encourages him to keep striking,” he added.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come after Russia carried out strikes on the war-torn country’s energy sector, including power generation and transmission facilities, with more than 320 jet-powered Shahed drones, loitering munitions, cruise and ballistic missiles. Power was reportedly cut for about 1 million people.
They also come as U.S. President Donald Trump signed on Friday an executive order that waived key sanctions on Russia — a decision that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, described as “an important and truly historic moment.” Trump’s move comes only a few days after he made a deal with Putin over supplying barrels of diesel, leaving European countries and Ukraine stunned.
“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely ignore Lindsey Graham’s bill, which was supposed to introduce truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” Zelenskyy said. “This bill could have helped a great deal, and it still can! But the law needs to actually work, and every vote for it matters.”

Russian missile strikes on Kharkiv injured 15 people, including three children, late Friday evening, Oct. 16, damaging residential high-rises and warehouse infrastructure, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) reported.

The blast ignited a fire spanning 100 square meters and caused structural damage to neighboring multi-story residential apartment buildings and adjacent facilities.
In total, the strikes produced four distinct fires across the impact perimeter. Specialized firefighting units and rescue teams from the DSNS contained and extinguished all four blazes during overnight operations.
Medical personnel and first responders treated 15 injured civilians at the scene and in municipal medical facilities, confirming that three children were among the wounded.
Overnight nationwide barrage and air defense operations
The strikes on Kharkiv formed part of an expansive overnight aerial assault conducted between Friday evening and Saturday morning, Oct. 17, combining ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and strike drones across several Ukrainian regions.
According to an operational summary issued by the Ukrainian Air Force Command, Russian forces launched ballistic missiles – including Iskander-M and KN-23 systems – from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions alongside occupied Crimea, Kh-22 and Kh-32 cruise missiles from Crimean airspace, four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk, and 332 unmanned aerial vehicles from multiple staging bases across Russia and occupied territories.

The drone assault incorporated a mix of Shahed loitering munitions – including 31 turbojet-powered variants – alongside S-8000 Banderol compact cruise munitions, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoy platforms.
Ukrainian air defense units, combat aviation, electronic warfare teams, and mobile interceptor groups downed or suppressed 293 aerial targets by 8:00 a.m. local time, including all four Kalibr cruise missiles and 289 strike and decoy drones, 23 of which were jet-powered models.
Military authorities confirmed that incoming munitions struck 22 distinct locations nationwide alongside falling debris from intercepted weapons.
Morning strikes on Zaporizhzhia
The Friday evening injuries in Kharkiv were followed early Saturday morning by strikes targeting urban infrastructure in southeastern Ukraine.
Russian forces launched several missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia shortly after 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, striking an open area surrounded by residential blocks. Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Head Ivan Fedorov confirmed that at least two civilians were injured in the attack, while the blast damaged three residential buildings and set multiple parked vehicles on fire.
The missile arrivals in Zaporizhzhia coincided with widespread air defense alerts issued across central and southern Ukraine, with air defense commands tracking ballistic trajectories toward Kryvyi Rih, Kamianske, and Dnipro in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

articles.title: Trump weighs in on Ukraine’s Starlink access
articles.body:
Trump weighs in on Ukraine’s Starlink access
US President Donald Trump claimed on Friday that he did not order restrictions on Ukraine’s military access to Starlink satellite services, adding that he did not believe SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had done so either.
Ukrainian state and military officials earlier this week accused SpaceX of abruptly restricting access to Starlink satellite communications services and Starshield, its military-grade version, which Kiev relies on for frontline drone operations. Musk responded that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government. The billionaire stressed that Starlink should be used only for civilian and defensive purposes, arguing that employing its systems for offensive operations would be “inappropriate for a commercial company.”
The development followed US President Donald Trump stepping up pressure on Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for surging global energy prices. Trump has also repeatedly urged the Ukrainian leader to hold a long-overdue presidential election.
At the same time, Washington lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports following talks with the Kremlin, prompting criticism from Zelensky. On Friday, the US President stated that he waived penalties aimed to target Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy, which had been signed into law just a month ago.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said when asked who had been behind the alleged suspension of the Starlink systems. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
Reuters reported on Thursday, citing officials briefed on the matter, that people “inside the White House” had instructed the Pentagon to impose speed restrictions on Starshield terminals. The report did not name the people who allegedly issued the directive, while a senior US official told Bloomberg at the time that Trump had not personally ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield.
On Friday, The Telegraph cited four sources familiar with the discussions as saying that Musk had approached Trump with the proposal to introduce speed limits on the system. One of the sources told the newspaper that Trump “agreed” with the suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to execute the slowdown.
The reports came as Washington continued to ramp up pressure on Kiev to accelerate efforts to reach a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this week, Zelensky claimed that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it continued to ignore Trump’s demands to halt strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials have also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes. The White House has not confirmed the claims.
Media reports emerged earlier this month that the US had also threatened to halt the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons to press authorities in Kiev to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier this week that Russia was unaware either of the Starlink slowdown for the Ukrainians or that intelligence sharing had been cut off. Peskov noted that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has persistently condemned Western military aid to Ukraine, arguing that it only serves to prolong the conflict without changing the outcome.

articles.title: Ukraine still can't intercept drones due to Starlink issues, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine still unable to intercept Russian drones due to Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump.
"Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored."
Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory.
"Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems."
"Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating"
Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.
Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia.
"Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters. CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.
Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire.
In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.
On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted: "Time for Zelensky to go."

articles.title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
articles.body:
Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
WASHINGTON/KYIV, Oct 17 - From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.
US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks.
Intensifying the discord, Trump waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelenskiy to say in social media posts that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.
The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow.
Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia.
Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said.
'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL
Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts.
Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month.
Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so.
Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people."
The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow.
The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote.
HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE
For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital.
Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters.
Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off.
Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was disrupted after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported on Thursday.
The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration.
Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom argue that Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow.
Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy.
“Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.” REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine downed four thousand seven hundred air targets
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defences destroyed more than 4,700 drones and missiles during September while repelling large-scale Russian attacks, and neutralised more than 48,000 tactical uncrewed aerial vehicles over the same month, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The figures, attributed to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, break down into a pattern dominated overwhelmingly by one-way attack drones. Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 types accounted for 2,722 of the interceptions and the jet-powered Shahed-238 for a further 1,935, with 1,009 reconnaissance drones and 719 Lancet loitering munitions also brought down.
Missile interceptions made up a far smaller share of the total, with Ukrainian defences stopping 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles, six Kh-59 and Kh-69 guided air-launched missiles, and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles. Another 86 S8000 Banderol missiles were destroyed.
The ministry said the targets were destroyed “through the efforts of aviation, surface-to-air missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defence Forces of Ukraine.”
On where the difficulty now lies, the department said: “Ballistic missiles remain a challenge for Ukraine’s air defense. At the same time, the enemy is increasingly using jet-powered drones that fly at speeds of around 400 km/h, reducing the time available to detect and intercept them.”
It added: “In addition, the enemy sends small groups of several jet-powered drones to different regions. To counter such targets, Ukraine uses aviation, among other means, and is developing innovative interception capabilities.”
Jet-powered Shaheds were shot down at nearly thirteen times the rate of every Russian missile type combined, which is a measure of how far the campaign has shifted away from missiles. A propeller-driven Shahed cruises at around 180 kilometres an hour and can be engaged by a gun truck, a helicopter or a cheap interceptor drone. At 400 kilometres an hour the engagement window halves, mobile fire groups lose much of their usefulness, and the problem starts to look more like intercepting a cruise missile than swatting a lawnmower.
Sending them in small packets to widely separated regions compounds the problem, because a defence designed around massed raids on a few cities has to be spread thinly to cover dispersed single-target attacks, and the aircraft Ukraine is using to run down the fast drones are the same F-16s and Mirages it needs for other tasks.
Evgeniy Khmara, the Ukrainian Defence Minister, raised munitions supply for the F-16 force in a recent conversation with German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, saying deliveries help ensure their effectiveness in shooting down Russian drones. The two also discussed protection of critical infrastructure and the need for more air defence assets including interceptors for the IRIS-T system.
Britain’s contribution to this problem has been concentrated on the cheap end, which is where the arithmetic works. The Lightweight Multirole Missile, built by Thales at Belfast and known in Royal Navy service as Martlet, has been supplied in quantity for counter-drone use, and the company confirmed this week that it has quadrupled production capacity at the site. Gravehawk, the British and Danish funded system that puts Soviet air-to-air missiles into a shipping container with a British sensor fit, was developed specifically to give Ukraine more launchers without waiting for Western interceptor stocks.

articles.title: Trump blocks new Russia sanctions days before they take effect
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has suspended a sweeping package of sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia just days before the measures were due to take effect, citing American national interests. The decision has drawn criticism from US lawmakers and praise from Moscow, further intensifying tensions between Washington and Kyiv.
Trump issued an executive order on Friday waiving several provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Congress passed with bipartisan support and the president signed into law in September.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The legislation was designed to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine by targeting Russian officials, financial institutions and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to transport oil despite Western restrictions.
It also authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported from major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, potentially affecting countries including China and India.
The new restrictions were scheduled to take effect on Sunday, 18 October, but Trump's order suspends their implementation until the administration determines that further action is appropriate.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump stated in the order.
The decision comes amid concerns that additional restrictions on Russian energy exports could drive global oil prices higher ahead of November's US midterm elections. Energy costs have already risen sharply amid the ongoing US-Israeli conflict with Iran, placing political pressure on the Trump administration.
The move was welcomed by Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy, who described the suspension as an "important and truly historic moment".
Dmitriev argued that implementing the sanctions would have severely damaged international markets and economic relations between Russia and the United States.
In Washington, Democratic Representative Don Beyer accused Trump of undermining congressional efforts to hold Moscow accountable.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.
The suspension follows another controversial decision by Washington to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in a claimed effort to reduce American and global fuel prices.
That agreement prompted criticism from a bipartisan group of US senators, including six Republicans, who warned that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's military operations in Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has similarly condemned the diesel arrangement, warning that additional revenue would flow into Russia while its invasion continues.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated further over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine halt the strikes, arguing that they contribute to higher international energy prices.
Following the collapse of a proposed energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed refinery attacks on Thursday after Russian forces continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump subsequently described the Ukrainian operations as a "disgrace" and renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy.
Ukrainian officials have reported disruptions to satellite communications used for drone operations, while Reuters reported, citing unnamed US and Western officials, that an order to restrict the Starshield system originated inside the White House.
Trump has denied personally ordering the restrictions and has rejected claims that Washington halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

articles.title: Europe Readies Post-Truce Ukraine Deployment Drill
articles.body:
At least 1,500 military personnel from the UK, France, and Germany will deploy to Poland in November to conduct specialized joint exercises simulating troop deployment and stabilization procedures in Ukraine in the event of a negotiated ceasefire, The Times reported.
The multinational maneuvers were formally announced by UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting following bilateral consultations with US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Thursday, Oct. 15.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Streeting confirmed that “hundreds” of British soldiers will participate in the deployment exercise alongside European counterparts.
“Next month, thousands of military personnel will take part in major exercises in Poland to ensure that we are ready to support the military training and post-war reconstruction that Ukraine will need,” Streeting stated.
According to defense sources cited by The Times, the exercise marks the first dedicated allied simulation designed specifically to prepare for a post-conflict phase in Ukraine, where the physical presence of European forces would serve as a conventional deterrent against renewed aggression.
Logistics, training, and deterrence protocols
Participating formations will rehearse cross-border transit logistics, rapid re-supply chains, and baseline sustainment operations – including forward food and fuel pipelines – under the framework of a prospective multinational peacekeeping or training commitment.
EU Tasks Commission to Bridge Ukraine’s €70B Funding Gap
Defense officials emphasized that the maneuvers do not indicate an imminent deployment of NATO troops into Ukrainian sovereign territory.
Instead, the exercise is engineered to validate technical protocols and joint command interoperability should a durable armistice or cessation of hostilities materialize.
The initiative highlights expanding coordination among European defense ministries to assume greater responsibility for continental security frameworks and wartime transition contingencies, ensuring rapid response capabilities if a ceasefire is formalized between Kyiv and Moscow.
Black Sea security requests and maritime friction
The planning for post-conflict deployment rehearsals in Poland arrives as NATO’s eastern and southeastern frontiers confront mounting operational challenges and maritime security friction.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria requested expanded defensive assistance from NATO on Oct. 16, asking the alliance to supply combat aircraft, air defense missile batteries, counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) systems, and regular air patrols following repeated drone attacks against merchant shipping transiting its Black Sea exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov confirmed that Sofia requested “the entire spectrum of available assets” to reinforce deterrence in the region, noting that regional partners Romania and the Baltic states confront comparable aerial and maritime vulnerabilities.
The security appeals followed consecutive drone strikes targeting civilian commercial shipping off the Bulgarian coastline throughout October.
On Oct. 6, strikes hit the commercial vessels Alfa Watan and Able within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, causing the Alfa Watan to sink and marking the first hostile kinetic attack inside the maritime economic perimeter of a NATO member state.
Subsequent strikes on Oct. 13 damaged the Maltese-flagged cargo vessel Chelsea 3 roughly 18 nautical miles off Byala and sank a second vessel near Krapets, prompting Bulgarian authorities to deploy additional missile batteries and drone-tracking systems along the coastline.

articles.title: Trump Halts Sweeping Russia Sanctions, Citing US National Interest
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday, Oct. 16, suspending sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump cited US national interests despite growing concerns that easing economic pressure on Moscow could help finance its war against Ukraine.
The executive order published by the White House waives major provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The suspended measures include additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as countries facilitating Moscow’s sanctions evasion.
The restrictions were scheduled to take effect Sunday, Oct. 18, under legislation designed to cut the energy revenues sustaining Russia’s invasion.
“As described further in section 4 of this order, I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote.
The decision follows his controversial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which eased restrictions on Russian fuel exports amid rising global energy prices.
It also comes as relations between Washington and Kyiv have deteriorated, with President Volodymyr Zelensky warning that allowing Russia to earn more from energy sales could strengthen Putin’s ability to continue the war.
Zelensky: Starlink Still Not Fully Restored, Disrupting Drone Defense and Frontline Supplies
Trump suspends 500% tariffs and penalties on Russian oil buyers
Under the Graham Act, Congress authorized extensive economic measures against Russia’s energy and defense industries, financial institutions, senior officials and networks helping Moscow circumvent Western sanctions.
The legislation also provided for steep tariffs against countries continuing to purchase Russian energy, extending the financial consequences of Moscow’s invasion to its major trading partners.
Trump’s order sets out three major tariff categories:
- An additional 500% duty on goods imported from Russia.
- A 100% duty on imports from the five largest buyers making new purchases of Russian oil or natural gas beginning Oct. 18.
- A 100% duty on goods from the five leading countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.
However, the order simultaneously waives those duties, preventing their immediate application.
The decision shields major Russian energy customers, potentially including China and India, from new US trade penalties as long as the waiver remains in effect.
The measures also targeted Russia’s so-called shadow fleet – tankers used to transport Russian oil despite Western efforts to restrict Moscow’s energy exports.
Trump’s order suspends specified new sanctions provisions but does not remove restrictions already imposed under separate executive authorities.
Trump invokes national interest exemption
The president relied on Section 115 of the Graham Act, which allows sanctions, restrictions and tariffs to be waived if the administration certifies that doing so serves US national interests.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump stated.
The legislation also requires a report explaining the basis for that determination.
The executive order confirms that the certification and accompanying report were submitted to Congress, but does not publicly provide a detailed explanation of why suspending the additional penalties would serve US interests.
The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or designated administration officials determine that further action is appropriate.
The order directs the US Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, to continue monitoring Russian energy purchases and sanctions evasion.
Although the administration retains authority to reconsider the waivers, no timetable for restoring the measures was announced.
Bipartisan backlash over sanctions relief
Trump’s decision follows mounting criticism from lawmakers in both parties over the administration’s earlier agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
In a bipartisan letter to the administration, senators warned that allowing Russian energy exports could provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance military operations against Ukraine.
The criticism has extended beyond Democrats to Republicans who supported stronger economic pressure on Putin.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina has questioned the administration’s approach to the Russia diesel agreement and its implications for legislation championed by the late Lindsey Graham.
Democratic lawmakers have also challenged Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions Congress approved.
Representative Don Beyer accused the president of yielding to Putin, while Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized the administration for undermining congressional efforts to pressure Russia.
The dispute raises broader questions about the effectiveness of sanctions legislation when its implementation depends on presidential discretion.
Although the Graham Act remains law, its national interest waiver gives the administration substantial authority to prevent the new restrictions from taking effect.
Diesel deal with Putin precedes broader sanctions reversal
The decision comes one week after Trump agreed to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports in exchange for additional fuel supplies intended to ease pressure on international energy markets.
The agreement was presented by Washington as a response to rising fuel prices, which have been affected by the ongoing US-Israeli war against Iran and disruptions to global energy supplies.
Under the arrangement, Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel into international markets.
The White House has defended the cooperation as necessary to stabilize prices for American consumers and businesses.
However, critics argue that increasing Russian energy sales could replenish Moscow’s revenues at a time when Western sanctions are intended to limit its ability to sustain the invasion of Ukraine.
Kyiv condemns sanctions relief as Russia continues attacks
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy, warning that additional revenues could strengthen Moscow’s ability to finance its invasion.
He called the diesel arrangement a “weak decision” and insisted that Russia should face increased economic pressure rather than concessions.
The dispute has coincided with Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries.
Trump described Kyiv’s renewed attacks as a “disgrace,” arguing that they were contributing to higher global energy prices.
Zelensky has defended Ukraine’s efforts to weaken Russian oil infrastructure, which generates revenue supporting Moscow’s military operations.
Ukraine has also accused Russia of continuing to target Ukrainian energy facilities despite discussions about a possible mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
During Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, European Council President António Costa rejected the idea of easing pressure on Moscow.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” Costa said.
“Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”

articles.title: Major Russian Strike on Vinnytsia Region Injures 6
articles.body:
Six people were injured and critical infrastructure was damaged during one of the largest Russian aerial assaults on Vinnytsia region since the start of the full-scale war, regional authorities reported on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Head of the Vinnytsia Regional Military Administration Nataliia Zabolotna confirmed on Facebook that Ukrainian air defense units intercepted 24 adversary strike drones over the region during the overnight engagement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Despite defensive interceptions, incoming munitions struck civilian targets and vital infrastructure facilities across the province, leaving six people wounded.
“We have damage to civilian and critical infrastructure. Six people were injured,” Zabolotna said.
“One person is in intensive care in serious but stable condition. Three people are in moderate condition, and two others sustained minor injuries. All are receiving necessary medical treatment.”
Emergency utility repairs
Following the strikes, utility repair crews and electrical dispatchers enacted emergency operational protocols to restore disconnected municipal life-support systems.
Zabolotna reported that critical infrastructure sites across the impacted districts were transferred onto backup emergency generators to sustain baseline services while repair teams worked to restore municipal electricity and potable water supply.
Regional authorities appealed directly to residents across Vinnytsia region to conserve electricity and avoid overloading the vulnerable power grid as reconnection efforts progress.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 16, 2026
“We urge residents of the region to switch on electrical appliances gradually and alternately as power is restored to prevent artificial overloads on the energy system,” Zabolotna stated.
Overnight nationwide barrage
The assault on Vinnytsia region formed part of a coordinated overnight Russian standoff barrage conducted between Friday evening and Saturday morning, combining ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hundreds of strike drones across Ukrainian territory.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force Command, Russian forces launched ballistic missiles – including Iskander-M and KN-23 systems – from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions alongside occupied Crimea, Kh-22 and Kh-32 cruise missiles from Crimean airspace, four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles from Novorossiysk, and 332 unmanned aerial vehicles from several launch staging grounds.
Ukrainian air defense units, combat aviation, electronic warfare forces, and mobile interceptor teams intercepted or suppressed 293 aerial targets by 8:00 a.m. on Saturday, including all four Kalibr cruise missiles and 289 strike and decoy drones.
The overnight bombardment inflicted casualties and infrastructure damage across multiple Ukrainian regions. In Kharkiv, missile strikes on the Nemyshlianskyi district late Friday evening wounded 15 civilians, including three children, while igniting four fires and heavily damaging residential apartment buildings and a commercial warehouse.
Early Saturday morning, Russian forces also fired missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia, striking an open area near residential blocks. Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Head Ivan Fedorov confirmed that two civilians were injured, with the explosions damaging three residential buildings and setting parked vehicles ablaze.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport on Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.
Missiles apparently launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi group struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify the attackers.
Read moreHouthis deny targeting holy city of Medina after Saudi Arabia says it intercepted missile
In Aden in southern Yemen, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Houthis. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week.
In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.

Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely throttled by Iran since the US and Israel launched attacks on the country in February.
With regional tensions and security threats raising concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies, Brent crude oil briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May.
Saudi Civil Defence authorities issued an alert early on Saturday for Abha in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border before sending an all-clear. Earlier they had issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Also early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes east of Yemen's northwestern city of Saada. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the area.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front as the Iran war has widened into a regional conflict. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited following a Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July, with the Iran-allied group targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.
The group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen in recent days, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

articles.title: Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine: Zelenskyy urges allies to pressure Russia as energy sites hit
October 17, 2026
Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.
His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.
What did Zelenskyy say?
In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.
"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.
"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.
Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.
He said Russia had "expanded its campaign against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch Ukraine's reserves and repair capacity as thinly as possible." 
Russia claims multiple infrastructure attacks
The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.
Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.
However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.
It said another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line, had also been struck.
Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed and 19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.
Russian state news agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.
Trump's sanctions waiver a boost for Putin: Zelenskyy
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.
On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.
The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."
"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.
Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."
Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

articles.title: US not to supply Ukraine with weapons at expense of its own security — columnist
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. The United States will not send weapons to Ukraine at the expense of security of its own armed forces in the Middle East, said Jude Russo, a columnist for the US magazine The American Conservative.
Commenting on reports about Ukraine’s shortage of missiles for Patriot air defense systems, the possible cessation of Washington’s transfer of intelligence data to Kiev, and the restriction of the Starlink satellite system, he said: "This is bad for Ukraine, although not altogether surprising. For months, the press has been full of ominous stories and analyses about the dire state of American munitions stockpiles after the US began its latest little jaunt in the Middle East."
"Reality is beginning to bite," the observer noted. In his opinion, even in the current conditions, the United States can continue the war with Iran without any special risks, but this "will come at the cost of readiness in other theaters." He said that a war with Iran "will always tend to demand more attention and resources than the proxy conflict in Europe. The US is not going to sacrifice the safety of its own military personnel and its own economic security for Ukraine."

articles.title: G7 pledges 260 million euros to repair Chornobyl’s shield after Russia pierced it. Full repair will require 500 million euros by 2030, before corrosion sets in
articles.body:
A Russian drone tore a hole in the shield over Chornobyl’s dead reactor. Now the G7 is paying to patch it.
The Group of Seven nations plans to allocate 260 million euros ($292 million) to repair the New Safe Confinement at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says on X.
The confinement, a 35-story steel arch sealing the reactor that exploded in the 1986 disaster, was damaged by a Russian drone strike in February 2025. Full restoration will cost at least 500 million euros, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) estimates, so the G7 pledge covers just over half, leaving about 240 million euros still to raise.
Shmyhal calls the decision an important step toward restoring nuclear safety at the plant, which the Russian strike had compromised. The money will go to priority work, including resealing the structure and restoring its ventilation system.
“Thank you to France and personally to Minister Roland Lescure for leadership in mobilizing international support,” Shmyhal says, crediting France and the EBRD with co-chairing the effort.
The night a drone pierced the sarcophagus
The damage dates to 14 February 2025. A Russian drone carrying a high-explosive warhead punched a hole through the arch’s roof and ignited a fire in the cladding, breaching the structure’s seal and ventilation.
The attack caused a 15 m² breach in the inner and outer cladding and damaged around 200 m² of panels.
"It was a targeted Russian attack on the Chornobyl station with a drone that is an analog of the Iranian Shahed," Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said at that time.
A bill only half-covered, and a 2030 deadline
The G7 money closes only part of the gap. Partners must still raise roughly 240 million euros more, and Ukraine hopes to secure it at a donor conference in Paris co-chaired by Ukraine, France and the EBRD, Shmyhal says.
The clock matters as much as the cost. The work must be finished by 2030 to limit corrosion and protect the arch’s 100-year design life, the EBRD says, turning a repair bill into a race against the rust the strike set loose.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Russia wants to deploy ballistic missile systems in Belarus to attack Ukraine's west
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Russia wants to deploy ballistic missile systems in Belarus to attack Ukraine's west
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Russians want to deploy not only drone relays but also ballistic missile systems in Belarus to attack Ukraine's west.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking to journalists
Quote from Zelenskyy: "Is there a threat of strikes and an increase in attacks on the western part of our state? Absolutely. Is Russia preparing for this? I think so.
Why are they constantly dragging Belarus into this, in my opinion? Because we know that they are placing relays on the territory of Belarus to use this corridor for drones and intensify the corresponding attacks.
But this is not enough for them; they need the support of [the self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander] Lukashenko to deploy other types [of weapons] on the territory of Belarus, including ballistic missiles. Undoubtedly, the deployment of ballistic missiles on the territory of Belarus would be a threat primarily to the western part of our state."
Details: Zelenskyy said the deployment of Russian ballistic missile systems would "directly drag Belarus into the war". He described this as "very dangerous for Belarus as well" and added: "God forbid they get dragged into this."
He also noted that Ukraine will bolster air defences in areas most frequently targeted by Russian attacks.
"Our approach to strengthening [air defence] is based on the following principle: the more attacks a region faces, the more air defence it gets. Of course, it is very important for us to strengthen air defence across the entire country. We will increase production of turrets, and our military will have to deploy them where the threat is greatest, providing greater protection there," he said.
