articles.title: Missiles hit Aden airport, Saudi coalition intercepts missile
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Missiles hit Aden airport as Saudi-led coalition intercepts missile headed for Yanbu
Missiles struck Aden International Airport in southern Yemen on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify those behind the attacks.
In Aden, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department said, blaming the Iran-aligned Houthi group. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. The Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility.
No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.
Yanbu is a key outlet for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, where heightened regional tensions and security threats have raised concerns over the safety of shipping.
Brent crude briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, as worries over escalating Middle East tensions raised concerns about tighter global supplies.
Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognised government south.
A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.
A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed and 327 wounded in what he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3.

articles.title: Zelensky: Russian forces attack more than 15 energy facilities
articles.body:
Zelensky: Russian forces attack more than 15 energy facilities
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky reported this on Facebook.
“Yesterday, the Russians launched one of their largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector: more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities in various regions of Ukraine were targeted. Restoration efforts are underway, involving all necessary services and all available resources from Ukrainian energy companies,” Zelensky wrote.
According to him, the situation was most critical in Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta, and Netishyn. Energy infrastructure in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, and Dnipropetrovsk regions, as well as other regions, was also targeted.
Zelensky noted that the Russians have escalated their anti-energy operation and are attempting to deplete Ukraine’s reserves and restoration capacity as much as possible.
“Between 7:00 p.m. yesterday and 7:00 a.m. today alone, more than 320 jet- and gasoline-powered ‘Shaheds,’ as well as loitering munitions, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, were used against our energy sector, our cities, and our communities. And although our soldiers manage to shoot down a significant portion of them, the sheer scale and relentlessness of the Russian strikes—particularly against the energy sector—unfortunately have many negative consequences,” he emphasized.
Zelensky reported that new support packages for Ukraine from European partners have already been prepared and thanked them for this. He also highlighted the importance of conveying information about these events to the United States.
“At a time when the Russians have launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, a decision was, unfortunately, made in America to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to exert truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war. This law could—and still can!—be of great help. But for the law to truly work, every vote in its favor matters,” Zelensky wrote.
He emphasized that the aggressor is trying to cause a blackout to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. To stop Russia, we must keep the pressure on it. At the same time, the U.S. easing pressure on the aggressor and offering financial incentives to Putin encourage him to continue the attacks.
“We must not give up our ground and must try to end the war—end it, rather than give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely. Thank you to everyone who is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine!” Zelensky added.
As reported, throughout the day on October 16, energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv, Kharkiv, Rivne, Volyn, and Odesa regions came under Russian attack.
On the night of and morning of October 17, the Russians attacked energy infrastructure in the Vinnytsia, Volyn, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi, and Kharkiv regions.

articles.title: Israel must treat the media war as seriously as Iran’s nuclear threat, Gil Hoffman says
articles.body:
Three years after Hamas’s October 7 attack, Israel is still fighting a war it was never prepared for, one in which the weapons are not missiles or tanks but headlines, social media posts, and the narratives that shape how the world sees the Jewish state.
For Gil Hoffman, a veteran political analyst who has spent much of his career examining how Israel is portrayed abroad, this battle is not simply a public relations issue, but a strategic threat that the country’s leadership has repeatedly failed to recognize.
Hoffman covered politics for The Jerusalem Post for nearly a quarter century, before taking over as executive director and executive editor of HonestReporting to “lead the fight for Israel on the media battlefield.”
He spoke with the Post this week in the wake of the publication of his new book, The Blood Libel Machine, which argues that the spread of anti-Israel narratives and the surge in global antisemitism were not simply spontaneous responses to the war, but the result of a premeditated information campaign that had been in the works for decades.
On October 7, 2023, that media battlefield took on a new urgency. As Hamas terrorists crossed into southern Israel, the images and accounts of the massacre spread quickly around the world.
Israel failed on a major front: The media landscape
Hoffman saw that Israel had been caught off guard in two distinct but interconnected arenas. In his book, he describes October 7 as not only a military and intelligence failure, but also a failure on the media front.
Three years on, he said, Israel still fundamentally misunderstands how to communicate with the world.
Israel’s failure to prepare for the media battlefield
“Hamas planned this war in order to impact public opinion around the world,” he said. “Their goal was not Nova, which they did not know about; it was New York, and Israel played into their hands. They wanted Israel to respond with what they could call disproportionate force, no matter what it would be, and return the Palestinian issue to the international agenda.”
Israel not having a plan on this front, just like it didn’t have a plan on the military front, has harmed the Jewish state “tremendously,” Hoffman added.
“Every day since October 7 has become easier on the military battlefield. Every day since October 7 has gotten progressively harder on the media one.”
The contrast is central to his book. Israel has devoted enormous resources to its military prowess, but Hoffman argues that successive governments have treated public diplomacy as a secondary concern, despite its potential influence on both domestic security and the security of Jewish communities abroad.
According to Hoffman, the problem begins at the highest levels of government.
“They did not realize they need to be taking into account how the decision they’re about to make in Gaza, in Iran, against Hezbollah, how these decisions are going to impact the Jews in Golders Green and in New York. They did not take it into account whatsoever.”
Another strategic failure Hoffman identified is Israel’s tendency to remain on the defensive rather than challenge the credibility and motivations of those shaping the international narrative.
Much of Israel’s media strategy, if there is one, has focused on rebutting misinformation, disputing facts and figures, and pointing out flaws in logic.
Hoffman said Israel needs to be much more on the offensive.
In his book, he lays out four necessary strategies he believes must work together: offensive and defensive messaging, both within the context of the conflict and beyond it.
“I count four. It makes a Venn diagram that works all together. If you’re missing out on any of the four, then it’s inadequate. So, yes, we need to be blackening the names of the people fighting against us.”
For example, Israel should be “outing” international anti-Israel figures who are accepting huge amounts of money from Qatar, Hoffman argued.
“We need to be outing that. It’s not legitimate, the way that Qatar is influencing the world. Al Jazeera is not a legitimate news organization. It’s a propaganda mouthpiece of a terrorist-supporting state. People need to know that. People need to know what they can and they can’t trust.”
Qatar occupies a prominent place in Hoffman’s analysis. The Gulf state, which has hosted Hamas political leaders and played a central role in negotiations involving Israel and Hamas, funds Al Jazeera, one of the most influential Arabic-language news networks in the world. Hoffman argues that Qatar’s financial and media influence warrants greater scrutiny.
The offensive strategy also needs to be employed more on college campuses, where, for a very long time, the pro-Israel groups have been trying to be “nice,” and Hoffman says they “need to be less nice because the anti-Israel organizations on their campus are not nice.”
He believes pro-Israel students and organizations need to be more assertive in challenging anti-Israel activism rather than relying primarily on dialogue and attempts to persuade those already strongly opposed to Israel.
This also connects to Qatar, given the extensive reporting indicating significant academic institutional ties between the Gulf state and US universities.
How international institutions shape the narrative
One of the most challenging aspects of this media fight is combating the dominant narrative disseminated by human rights bodies and NGOs, Hoffman said.
The United Nations, Oxfam, Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders, and others have been instrumental in legitimizing the anti-Israel rhetoric used in public and private spaces. Because of these organizations, buzzwords such as “genocide,” “apartheid,” and “ethnic cleansing” have become normalized in day-to-day discourse and in international media outlets.
Hoffman said he wanted to speak to journalists who covered the conflict during the war and “give them the benefit of the doubt.” He said he asked them why they believed Hamas.
“They said, ‘No, we didn’t believe anything from Hamas. We believe the organizations [like the UN].’ And they believed Hamas.
“These organizations were the ones who spread the propaganda and sanitized what a terrorist organization [Hamas] told them. Then the media quote these reputable organizations around the world, and it becomes a vicious circle. As Gerald Steinberg, the founder of NGO Monitor, understood way back at the Durban [Conference], this was going to cause damage to Israel, and now the entire world needs to understand that.”
The Durban reference is significant. At the 2001 UN World Conference Against Racism in South Africa, an accompanying NGO forum became the focus of controversy over antisemitism and the portrayal of Israel. Its declaration described Israel as an apartheid state and accused it of genocide and ethnic cleansing, language that would become increasingly prominent in subsequent campaigns against the Jewish state.
In Hoffman’s view, the events surrounding Durban were not an isolated episode but an early indication of how human rights terminology could be used as part of a broader campaign to delegitimize Israel.
“So, that’s part of that blood libel machine, the way in which – wittingly or unwittingly, and, unfortunately, too often wittingly – these NGOs were part of it. So the blood libel machine is the media. It is Qatar. It is Hamas. It is the anti-Israel organizations around the world.”
Fighting back against the machine
Fighting this is an uphill battle, partly because these organizations are viewed internationally as the beacons of justice and paragons of morality. It is not easy to convince skeptics that their findings and public statements should be subjected to the same scrutiny as those of governments and other parties.
“It’s hard, but we need to be constantly putting out facts,” Hoffman continued. “We know how many tons of aid we’re giving to Gaza. We know what everything Israel did unprecedentedly to help an enemy combatant in the time of war. We know how much effort Israel made to minimize civilian casualties. Little by little, we can chisel away at this false narrative that has been hoisted upon the world.”
Hoffman’s determination to remain optimistic is a recurring theme throughout both the book and the interview, even as he describes the scale of the challenge facing Israel.
“I didn’t want to write a book of gloom and doom. I wanted to write a book that would give people hope.
“That’s why the subtitle of the book is Exposing the anti-Israel Hate Network, and How to Fight Back. I give people 30 different tools they can use, whether it’s in mainstream media, social media, or AI platforms.”
Rather than leaving readers with a diagnosis of the problem, Hoffman devotes a substantial portion of the book to practical action. He does not believe it is too late for Israel to turn the tide.
“It’s not too late. Every day, every single person on social media and even people who aren’t on social media, in the checkout line of the grocery store, everybody can make an impact.
“I don’t view it as this mountain that’s insurmountable. I believe in celebrating incremental success. And we, every day, can change minds. Not of the most extreme people, but of the overwhelming majority.”
One way he suggests people take action is by engaging more critically with international media and holding them accountable when they find incorrect or biased reporting.
“People often ask me, should I cancel my subscription to The New York Times and other media outlets for being anti-Israel?
“I say absolutely not. You need to be reading it. If you want to hurt them, then read them more carefully. If you see something problematic, send it to the media watchdogs like HonestReporting or to journalists themselves, or send it to their local media and point out that their rival had made an error. And that’s all part of regaining deterrence on the media battlefield.”
This approach is shaped by his years in journalism and media monitoring. Rather than disengage from outlets they distrust, Hoffman argues, readers should become more informed, attentive consumers of their reporting.
He cited an example of when, during coverage of the release of the final 20 living hostages in October 2025, CNN reporter Christiane Amanpour claimed that Israeli hostages were treated “better than the average Gazan” because Hamas used them as bargaining chips.
Someone flagged the comment, and Hoffman himself then contacted Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, who contacted CNN and requested that she be held accountable.
Amanpour subsequently apologized, calling her comments insensitive and wrong.
“That came from ordinary people who were watching and made sure that we would realize this. And so people can have that role when they see things that are egregious.”
Social media also has the technology for users to critically engage. For example, users on X/Twitter can add community notes on posts that are incorrectly presented or are missing key information.
Looking to Israel’s next government
While Hoffman does believe responsibility can rest with individual news consumers, his criticism ultimately returns to Israel’s political leadership and its failure to treat public diplomacy as an essential element of national security.
While citizens may help challenge misleading narratives, only the government has the authority and tools to establish a coordinated, long-term communications strategy, one that anticipates the international consequences of its actions rather than responding after the damage has been done.
“They need to be taking this just as seriously as the nuclear threat from Iran, because it’s an existential threat to the future of the State of Israel and the Jewish people around the world.
“And they need to be caring about the way every decision they make is perceived abroad.”
With Israel’s October 27 elections approaching, the question is whether a new government, regardless of its political makeup, will be prepared to invest in the media battlefield as seriously as it invests in conventional security.
“It doesn’t matter who wins the election. They all need to make sure the next government allocates just as much, if not more, funding to media strategy and public diplomacy. They need to have people ready 24/7 to go on the media and explain what’s going on here, in every language imaginable.
“The embassies and consulates abroad are dreadfully underfunded. And that needs to be changed, because those are the people who are building the relationships with the people there on the ground and with the media.”
Hoffman makes the case that the fight over Israel’s international reputation will not end when the fighting on the ground does. It will continue in newsrooms, universities, online platforms, and in day-to-day communication.
And while governments bear the most responsibility for preparing Israel to confront that challenge, Hoffman’s resounding message is that the battlefield is no longer theirs alone. Its outcome will also depend on whether those watching from the sidelines are willing to take action.

articles.title: Year-old startup wins spot in U.S. Army interceptor fly-off
articles.body:
- Furientis was selected as one of four vendors for a U.S. Army fly-off at the end of fiscal 2027 for a second IFPC Inc 2 interceptor.
- The year-old startup recently won its first funded Pentagon contract, raised $25 million, and unveiled a CAML launcher with Rheinmetall at AUSA.
Furientis, a missile startup founded just last year, has been picked as one of four companies to fly interceptors in a U.S. Army shoot-off at the end of fiscal 2027, competing to supply a second missile for the service’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 air defense system.
Co-founder and CEO Brody Franzen announced the selection, describing it as a downselect for a fly-off at the end of a fiscal year that closes on Sept. 30, 2027, without naming the other three companies chosen.
The Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2, or IFPC Inc 2, is the U.S. Army’s mid-range air defense system for protecting bases and troops from cruise missiles, drones, rockets and artillery. Its truck-mounted Enduring Shield launcher, built by Leidos subsidiary Dynetics, now fires RTX’s AIM-9X Sidewinder, and the U.S. Army has spent the past few years looking for a second, more capable missile that can handle fast, low-flying cruise missiles and be built in larger numbers.
Lockheed Martin and a team of Boeing and Anduril are already competing in the formal second-interceptor program, which moved into its demonstration phase in September after Rafael’s U.S. subsidiary was not selected to continue. At the Association of the U.S. Army conference this week, Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the service’s portfolio acquisition executive for fires, said the U.S. Army would open a parallel path for companies that missed that first cut but kept investing in their own designs, inviting them to bring missiles to the range for a shoot-off in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Breaking Defense reported, and Furientis’ selection appears to be part of that track.
Franzen and Aris Simsarian, both former engineers at Virgin Orbit and Castelion, founded Furientis in 2025 in the Los Angeles area to build interceptors designed for mass production from readily available parts. The company puts final assembly time at about 30 minutes and says it flight-tests prototypes roughly every two weeks instead of spending years on design before flying.
The startup came out of stealth in May with a $5 million pre-seed round, and on Oct. 6 it announced both a $25 million seed round led by Benchmark and its first funded government contract, a prototyping agreement with the U.S. Department of War for a 100-mile-range interceptor intended for homeland defense.
According to Franzen, the IFPC selection capped a busy two weeks in which Furientis flew its first horizontal flight test on a government range for the U.S. Army’s low-cost interceptor effort and, at AUSA, unveiled a containerized launcher developed with Rheinmetall for the U.S. Army’s Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher program.
He credited the U.S. Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires and its defensive fires team, led by Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, for opening the door to nontraditional vendors and giving them the resources to speed up development, and said Furientis is now hiring as it prepares its interceptor for the shoot-off due by the end of September 2027.

articles.title: Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
articles.body:
Representative Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced bipartisan legislation on Friday, Oct. 16, to prohibit the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s commercial diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The draft measure, titled the “Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act,” aims to dismantle the administrative mechanisms facilitating Russian petroleum transactions, mandate sanctions against the Russian energy industry, and restrict federal financial backing for related enterprises, according to an official announcement by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The legislative initiative explicitly prohibits the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russian energy projects, revokes all related general licenses issued by the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), and restricts executive agencies from issuing comparable sanctions exemptions in the future.
Meeks stated that the commercial agreement does not alleviate domestic economic pressures for American citizens, arguing that consumers are confronting elevated costs resulting from the administration’s military conflict with Iran.
Concurrently, the senior lawmaker warned that opening US and global markets to Russian diesel provides Moscow with critical hard-currency earnings that sustain military strikes against Ukrainian civilians.
Trump Denies Role in Slowing Ukraine’s Military Starlink
“At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine,” Meeks said in a statement.
“This goes against everything the United States stands for. Congress must act. Every Member of Congress who claims to be outraged by this should join in passing this legislation.”
Bipartisan congressional pushback against energy accommodations
The introduction of Meeks’ bill accelerates a coordinated bipartisan effort on Capitol Hill to challenge the administration’s commercial accommodations toward Moscow.
The move follows legislative action initiated earlier in the week by Republican Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, who began drafting the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” to establish a comprehensive statutory prohibition against importing Russian oil and refined hydrocarbons.
Lawmakers across both parties have criticized the administration for providing financial lifelines to the Kremlin’s defense sector while Ukrainian civilian and municipal energy networks face sustained long-range bombardments ahead of the winter heating season.
Under the framework announced by the White House following an Oct. 9 telephone call between Trump and Putin, Russia agreed to deliver commercial diesel fuel onto international markets through 2027. To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The commercial pivot drew immediate pushback from Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized the timing of the arrangement as a “smokescreen” while Ukrainian and European negotiators were conducting multilateral peace discussions with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Executive suspension of Graham Act sanctions
The legislative drive arrives immediately following Trump’s signature on Friday, Oct. 16, of an executive order waiving major statutory sanctions and trade tariffs targeting the Russian Federation just 48 hours before they were scheduled to take effect.
The presidential waiver suspended key enforcement mechanisms enacted under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.
The statute had established severe economic penalties designed to cut off revenues underwriting the Russian war effort, scheduled to enter into force on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Among the measures suspended by Trump’s order were an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports, alongside mandatory 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas, such as China and India.
The waiver also suspended secondary tariffs on the five leading nations identified as facilitating the evasion of Russian petroleum sanctions, while halting prospective enforcement actions against Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of tankers.
In the executive order, Trump asserted that waiving the Graham Act’s trade restrictions and duties aligned with US national interests, defending the step as necessary to manage global energy benchmarks.

articles.title: Ukraine's General Staff confirms strike on Russian drone plant in Rostov Oblast – photo
articles.body:
Ukraine's General Staff confirms strike on Russian drone plant in Rostov Oblast – photo
Ukrainian defence forces have struck Roboavia, a plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast that manufactures attack drones and reconnaissance UAVs for the Russian military.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Details: Ukrainian forces attacked the Roboavia plant near the settlement of Khutor Lenina on Friday 16 October. The General Staff confirmed a strike on a production and storage building.
Quote from the General Staff: "The strike on the infrastructure of this company, which develops and manufactures unmanned aerial vehicles for the Russian army, is aimed at disrupting UAV production and supply to Russian forces."
Details: The Ukrainian military also confirmed a strike on a logistical supplies warehouse belonging to a unit of a Russian missile brigade near the settlement of Latyshi, Bryansk Oblast, on 12 October.
Quote from the General Staff: "Strikes against such facilities are an exercise of Ukraine's inherent right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter and are aimed at reducing the military, economic and technological potential of the Russian Federation."
Details: The Roboavia plant in Rostov Oblast develops and manufactures Sarych UAVs equipped with video and thermal imaging surveillance. It also produces Klin loitering munitions, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine's War&Sanctions project explained.
The plant is part of the Era Military Innovation Complex, a Russian Defence Ministry project aimed at developing advanced weapons. Roboavia is subject to Ukrainian sanctions.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Defence Intelligence of Ukraine had released an interactive 3D model and information about the main elements and components of the Klin loitering munition produced by Roboavia.

articles.title: Now-ousted US general warned of defense munition shortage months before Iran war - report
articles.body:
A now-ousted US general warned that the American military was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage could last for at least five years in the months before the war with Iran began, according to a CBS News report on Thursday.
Multiple US officials familiar with the matter told CBS that Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George’s risk analysis was included in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan in late December.
George was ousted by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in April in the midst of the war with Iran.
According to CBS, George warned that both Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) battery and Patriot missile stockpiles would stay strategically low until at least 2030.
Anonymous US officials explained that George’s assessment stemmed from multiple factors, including the transfer of Patriot systems to Ukraine, munitions expended while defending Israel, and reduced defense industry production.
Officials told CBS that the US military does possess a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, such as Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM) and Small Diameter Bombs.
Over 50% of Patriot, THAAD interceptor stockpiles reportedly expended
Among the arms at critically low stock levels is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 interceptor, a surface-to-air munition designed to destroy ballistic and cruise missiles mid-air.
Patriot PAC-3 orders have an average delivery time of over three years, CBS cited the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) as estimating in April. Defense contractors can take over four years to deliver a new shipment of THAAD interceptors.
CSIS estimated that prior to the Iran war, when George made his assessment, the US may have had around 2,300 Patriot interceptors. Between 1,050 and 1,430 interceptors, or up to 61% of prewar inventory, may have been expended during the war with Iran.
According to CSIS, pre-war THAAD stockpiles included about 355 interceptors. Between 190 and 290 of the munitions were allegedly used in the war, potentially using up 82% of the inventory.
Stockpiles could take four years to replenish, US official says
While American defense contractors have made moves to increase production of THAAD and Patriot interceptors, a US official told CBS that even if no more munitions were used, it could take until 2030 for the stockpiles to be fully replenished.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell denied the reports of munitions shortages in a statement to CBS, stating that the US has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the president's choosing."

articles.title: U.S. Air Force adds drone-mimicking firm to adversary pool
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded KestrelX, A2G International and Fleet Adversary Support and Training places on a $5.4 billion adversary air and close air support contract.
- Work runs across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029, with only $3,000 obligated at award and funding to follow through task orders.
The U.S. Air Force has added three small companies to a contract worth up to $5.4 billion for privately flown “Red Air” adversary aircraft and close air support training, including a firm that flies small planes made to mimic enemy drones and cruise missiles.
KestrelX of Driggs, Idaho, A2G International of Melbourne, Florida, and Fleet Adversary Support and Training of St. Augustine, Florida, each received a place on the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract for the Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support program, the U.S. Department of War said. The Air Combat Command Acquisition Management and Integration Center at Langley Air Force Base, Virginia, awarded the deals on Oct. 15 after a competition in which three offers were received. Only $3,000 was obligated at signing, with money to flow later through individual task orders.
Under the program, private companies supply aircraft and pilots that play the enemy, or Red Air, against U.S. fighter crews in training, and fly close air support sorties so joint terminal attack controllers on the ground can practice calling in airstrikes. Work will take place across the continental United States through Oct. 8, 2029.
The new awards carry the same $5.4 billion ceiling and a nearly identical end date as the second Combat Air Force Contracted Air Support contract, which the U.S. Air Force awarded in September 2024 to eight established adversary air companies, including Airborne Tactical Advantage Company, Draken International, Top Aces and Tactical Air Support. Those firms compete with one another for task orders under the vehicle, and the original version, awarded in 2019, had a $6.4 billion ceiling.
KestrelX brings a different kind of aircraft to that pool. The company, founded by former U.S. Navy fighter and test pilot Don Moseley, flies small jets and light propeller planes modified to replicate drones and cruise missiles, and it has played those threats in exercises such as Northern Strike in Michigan. Last month, the U.S. Navy hired KestrelX under a contract worth up to $9.99 million to supply low-observable target aircraft and engineering support for training exercises.
A2G International describes itself as an operator of manned and unmanned aircraft that provides airborne intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance services to U.S. and foreign government customers.
Contracted Red Air grew as the U.S. Air Force ran short of its own aggressor aircraft and did not want to tie up front-line fighters, particularly F-35s, playing the enemy in training. A 2021 Government Accountability Office report found that the U.S. Air Force planned for adversary air contracts to serve as a bridge, with their use expected to phase out around 2030 as the service builds up its own aggressor squadrons and explores new crewed and uncrewed adversary aircraft.
Each of the three new companies will now be able to compete for task orders under the contract through October 2029.

articles.title: Ukraine cannot be forced to surrender, says commander whose brigade destroyed 57,000 Russian targets, as US pressure and Russian missiles test its will
articles.body:
Ending the war by forcing Ukraine to capitulate is impossible, the commander of the 429th “Achilles” Unmanned Systems Brigade, Yurii Fedorenko, said in an interview with 24 Kanal.
His statements came as Ukraine absorbed the fallout from the US-Russia diesel deal that saw its Starlink throttled and US intelligence lapse, a gap tied to a strike that killed three in Kyiv.
Achilles is a volunteer unit formed in the first days of the full-scale invasion, built around aerial reconnaissance and drone strikes and credited with more than 57,000 strikes. Fedorenko, its commander, was named a Hero of Ukraine in January 2026.
Fedorenko says he believes that there would be no “miraculous de-escalation,” and now argues that neither pressure from Washington nor Russian missiles can break the country’s will to fight for its liberty.
Russia will keep terrorizing Ukrainians with ballistic missiles, jet drones and Shaheds, and no near-term shift in US policy will stop it, Fedorenko stresses, so Ukraine will keep defending itself and striking back. A lasting energy ceasefire, he added, will not hold.
“Ukrainian society is ready to defend itself and to uphold its right to life by force,” he says, arguing that the Kremlin’s mouthpieces, and those working for third countries, have misjudged the mood in Ukraine.
No measure, he insists, could force Ukraine to capitulate in the short term.
Why the US election could swing the pendulum back
Fedorenko sees the political balance shifting after the US vote. President Donald Trump will probably not hold the majority he once had, making it harder for him to take domestic decisions alone, he notes. Even foreign policy, a presidential prerogative, will have to reckon with that balance.
If Trump must bargain with Democrats to pass domestic measures, that will shape the wider picture, Fedorenko argues. He stopped short of predicting impeachment, calling that the wrong framing, but cautioned that decisions already taken could be reviewed, challenged and overturned in the courts.
“I am firmly convinced we will get through the difficulties dictated by circumstances, including those arising across the ocean,” he says.
A cold shower for Europe that could help Ukraine
The US turn toward Moscow has jolted Europe, in Fedorenko’s view. American threats to leave NATO or rewrite how it shares the burden landed on European leaders like a cold waterfall, he recounts, pushing each state to ask how it would stand if the US walked away and to treat the Russian threat as one standing at its own borders, no longer a problem confined to Ukraine.
That alarm can work in Kyiv’s favor, drawing more weapons, defense financing and economic support from European partners, Fedorenko argues.
The same logic drives the satellite question. Ukraine cannot build a Starlink alternative alone, lacking its own space program, so the answer is collective, with NATO states pooling launches into a shared network, he explains. Russia is taking the other path with its “Rassvet” system, much of it, in fact, built by China, and if Moscow and Beijing get there first, he warns, the fallout would reach far beyond Ukraine.

articles.title: Independent Scotland would leave UK forces their kit
articles.body:
EXCLUSIVE – An independent Scotland would, the Scottish National Party believe, have a legitimate claim on its proportionate share of British military equipment but would decline to exercise it if taking the kit caused serious problems for what remained of the United Kingdom, the SNP Westminster leader told me when I sat down with him to chat all things defence.
Dave Doogan, the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, said the ownership position is clear even if the practical answer is not: “It’s important to remember that we own the assets, all of them proportionately, at the disposal of the UK defence forces, and so we’ve got a call on them. But why would we make problems for the UK by taking our share?”
He set that against the state of the British inventory, where he argues the margin for giving anything away has long since gone: “You know as well as I do that there is very little redundancy in any platform in the United Kingdom. You know, just look at what they were trying to do to get a functioning Type 45 out to the Mediterranean recently. If we think that there are squadrons of Typhoons up and down these islands ready to go at a moment’s notice, that’s not how it is.”
On that basis he ruled out pressing a claim that damaged the rest of the UK, telling me “So if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
Division of assets has been one of the hardest parts of the independence argument to pin down since 2014, when the Scottish Government’s white paper assumed Scotland would inherit a share of equipment and the then British government declined to negotiate before a vote. The eight per cent figure Doogan uses reflects Scotland’s rough share of the British population, which was the basis the 2014 prospectus worked from.
Indeed, his point about redundancy lands on a fleet that has been audited repeatedly on exactly that question. The Royal Navy’s six Type 45 destroyers have spent much of the past decade affected by the propulsion problems now addressed through the Power Improvement Project.
Doogan expects the negotiation to be conducted without rancour once the constitutional question is settled, and said the hostility between the two governments is a product of the constitutional argument itself: “That’s the world that we will actually enter after independence. It will be about constructive and mature discussion about here’s where we were, here’s where we are, where do we want to get to, and how do we do that in the best interests of an independent Scotland and the rest of the UK. Because this enmity that exists just now is a function of trying to keep the UK together. Once Scotland’s out of the UK, that enmity has no purpose anymore, and we’ll work together like grown-up and respectful states.”
He argued that cooperation would follow from self-interest on both sides, and that the rest of the UK would deal with Scotland as it deals with everywhere else it once governed: “Let’s not pretend for one minute that the United Kingdom, once all the heat has gone out of an independence debate and Scotland has chosen to be independent, the rest of the UK will cooperate with Scotland just in the same way it cooperates with every other entity and jurisdiction that used to be governed from London. It’s entirely predictable, because it’s to England’s and the rest of the UK’s self interest to cooperate with Scotland, and it’s in Scotland’s interest to cooperate with the rest of the UK.”
The loss of jurisdiction over the northern half of the island would present a problem, he accepted, and one he does not expect to be handled adversarially: “If the SNP or I have got anything to do with that, that won’t be a challenge because we’ll approach it in a cooperative way. How we do that is up for discussion. A brand new independent Scotland would not want to be undefended, but the rest of the UK would not wish a brand new independent Scotland to be undefended either.”
On the deterrent, Doogan said an independent Scotland would have no further locus once the system left Scottish waters, and would take no view on what Westminster did with it afterwards: “It’s not a Scottish asset or system, it’s a UK asset or system. And so what they choose to do with it, where they choose to berth it, whether they choose to sustain and renew it going forward into the future, that’s entirely up to the rest of the UK. Scotland will have no role in that. We’ll respect their sovereignty and their freedom of decision, and they’ll respect ours.”
The kit Scotland would be declining to take is itself under question in his view, and he turned to the surface fleet while discussing the Type 32 frigate, the conceptual class folded into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel programme without a commitment on where it would be built: “If I’m being honest and being fair, there is now a serious question mark about how many big grey ships you put on the surface of the sea, and how expensive and challenging it is to defend these assets now.”
He went on to set out the arithmetic that worries him, with the air defence destroyers tied to the carriers and the frigates left to look after themselves: “I don’t doubt the capabilities of Type 45, old as it is. It’s still a very potent warship, assuming it’s actually able to move itself, which is not guaranteed with 45. But it’s going to be busy defending two hulking great aircraft carriers, and so 31 and 26 are going to have to do a job defending themselves. That looks increasingly expensive against a volley, literally volley, of inexpensive, very hard to intercept drones.”
That point about escorts protecting themselves runs into an arithmetic problem the whole alliance is grappling with, because a Sea Ceptor round costs a great deal more than the one-way attack drones now being fired in salvoes at ships in the Red Sea and the Black Sea, and the Royal Navy has been working through directed energy and gun-based answers, including DragonFire, for exactly that reason. The Type 45s carry Sea Viper and Aster for area air defence, the capability the carriers depend on, and the fleet has six of them.
Doogan was also blunt about the policy architecture that was supposed to keep the yards busy into the next decade, recalling the ministerial appointments and slogans that have come and gone during his time in the Commons: “I’ve only been in Parliament seven years, and I remember when there was a shipbuilding czar. It was actually Ben Wallace, the Secretary of State for Defence. Not heard much about a shipbuilding czar recently. I remember when it was all about a shipbuilding pipeline. It was an end to boom and bust was what it was going to be. Well, it just goes to show you that those words are easy. What’s difficult is putting the resource in place to make sure that that happens.”
Doogan accepted that competing orders internationally is the straightforward part of the problem, “An anti-boom and bust and an actual pipeline of work, especially when you’re building grey ships, you have to compete it. Unfortunately, you have to compete it internationally. That’s easy. Let’s have, like, a no-brainer. What’s harder is to find the budget.”
On the wider state of conventional forces, he described a force he believes is being hollowed out around the edges, and listed what he sees when he looks at it: “If our soldiers were delighted, if our airmen felt that they had a purpose and that they could get more than a couple of flying hours a month, if our combat aircraft were properly armed, if we stopped buying systems that are fitted for but not with, because we can’t afford to put the missiles in the launch tubes that these systems have, if we weren’t practising launching artillery with two shells a day or a session, because there isn’t enough.”
He acknowledged where some of the ammunition has gone, while arguing that the replenishment should have followed: “Some of that, of course, is because we’ve sent so much artillery to Ukraine. But shells aren’t complex. We should be replenishing them, and it’s unfortunate that that money is just not there.”
Doogan put a figure on the shortfall he believes the Chancellor is facing, and drew a line around the nuclear enterprise while doing it: “You’ll need to find an extra fifteen to twenty billion for defence, and that’s going to be a real challenge. And that’s fifteen, twenty billion for the whole of defence outside the nuclear enterprise.”
The Type 32 was announced by Boris Johnson in November 2020 as a fifth-generation class of general purpose frigates intended to follow Type 31, and it never progressed beyond concept before being absorbed into the Future Cruiser Combat Vessel work that is now running alongside the Type 83 destroyer replacement for Type 45. Rosyth has gone from assembling the Queen Elizabeth class carriers to building the five Type 31 frigates in the Venturer Building, and the sustainability of that drumbeat after the Type 31 order runs out has been a persistent concern in Fife.
Talking about British kit and Scottish yards at this length is itself a change, and Doogan has been pushing his own party in that direction for years against a habit he describes as widespread across Scotland: “Within the SNP more generally, there is a kind of tacit reluctance to engage with defence issues, for a lot of people in Scotland, not just in the SNP. Defence in Scotland begins and ends with the deterrent. There’s an awful lot more to defence in Scotland than the deterrent. But conventional defence is really important, and I’ve worked really hard to try and get that up the SNP’s agenda.”
He called the shift a positive thing and cited the First Minister’s recent visit to Babcock at Rosyth, along with a run of further visits by SNP elected members to defence establishments in Scotland, both completed and upcoming. He traced the argument back to the party’s NATO policy and what he thinks it obliges a government to do: “SNP policy is to be part of NATO. If you want to be part of NATO, you have to accept that peace and security doesn’t land at your feet. And if you don’t ensure by your own words, deeds and resources that you can do everything you possibly can to secure your peace and security, well then you’re not much use as a government to your people, and you’re not much use to your allies as a partner in peace and security.”
He said the case lands with colleagues when it is put to them directly, and that it follows from something the party already accepts about the armed forces: “When you speak to people about it, that’s not a controversial view in the SNP, and I think that’s a good thing, and it’s a work in progress, and people I think are accepting of it because actually it’s an extrapolation of, if we hold our men and women in uniform in the highest of regard, then we must hold what they do in the highest of regard, and if we do that, then we have to accept that they need to be equipped, and that allows us to hold defence manufacturers in high regard too.”
Doogan spent his career in defence engineering, working on Ministry of Defence helicopters, before entering Parliament in 2019. Asked what he would say to a young person in Scotland weighing up a career in the sector, he was unequivocal: “Any young person looking at possibly taking a job in engineering, do it. And getting a job in engineering and defence, do it, because if for no other reason, in defence you’re operating to the highest of standards in the best of conditions often, and those skills are in huge demand globally and domestically. So it’s a very good employment opportunity.”
He had made a related point at an industry event the previous evening, taking issue with the way politicians talk about employment: “Politicians have a habit of just talking about jobs in abstract, as though all jobs are equal. All jobs are not equal. Engineering jobs are an extremely attractive career proposition, and defence engineering jobs in particular are an extremely attractive employment proposition. So anybody thinking about that, I would say go on ahead and do it, because the more people that repopulate our defence sector in Scotland, the better.”
The same session covered the sub-threshold threats facing Britain and Scotland, which he put in terms of the damage they do to ordinary economic life: “Talking about the range of sub-threshold grey zone threats that we face, which aren’t in themselves the end of the world, but are a serious impediment. See Jaguar Land Rover, serious impediment to our freedom and liberty and our economy and people’s jobs.”
Doogan’s comments come a day after the Scottish Government confirmed it will match the ten million pounds offered by the Ministry of Defence to establish two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland, ending a wait of seven months since the offer was made in March. Alyn Smith, the Innovation Minister, wrote jointly with Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn to confirm the money, with sites to be allocated in the east and west of the country covering defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology.
The sector Doogan wants repopulated employs a substantial number of people across Scotland. BAE Systems builds the Type 26 frigates at Govan and Scotstoun, Babcock assembles the Type 31 at Rosyth, Leonardo produces radar and electronic warfare equipment in Edinburgh, Thales builds optronics and missile systems at Govan, and Raytheon operates at Glenrothes. All of them compete for the same welders, electrical technicians and systems engineers, and all of them have warned about the pipeline.
The SNP’s position on defence has moved considerably over the past two years, with the Programme for Government committing to a responsible defence industrial growth programme, a formulation that keeps public money away from munitions while backing the wider sector. Doogan describes the shift inside his own party as unfinished work.

articles.title: Poland scrambles aircraft as Russia strikes western Ukraine amid Warsaw-Trump rift
articles.body:
Jo Harper
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Poland scrambled military aircraft on Saturday as Russia launched fresh strikes on western Ukraine.
Polish and allied aircraft were deployed to protect Polish airspace as Russian attacks targeted areas near the NATO member’s eastern border, according to Poland’s armed forces.
The precautionary move came as Washington and Warsaw increasingly appeared to be moving in different directions over Russia. Trump on Saturday waived key Russia-related sanctions and tariffs due to take effect under the recently adopted Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, saying the move was in US national interest. The law had been intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The waiver followed a US-Russia diesel deal that has drawn criticism from Kyiv and some European leaders, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the agreement would provide Moscow with financial relief while Russia continues its attacks on Ukraine.
Warsaw has maintained a harder line. Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski this week criticized restrictions affecting Ukraine’s Starlink service and questioned whether Elon Musk was “playing politics” with a system that is crucial to Ukrainian defense. Poland pays for Starlink subscriptions used by Ukraine.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk has also repeatedly argued that continued pressure on Russia and support for Ukraine are central to Polish and European security.
Poland has adopted an increasingly active air-defense posture since a series of incidents linked to Russia’s war in Ukraine. In September 2025, Polish and allied aircraft were deployed during Russian strikes on western Ukraine, while Poland later became the first NATO member to shoot down Russian drones after incursions into its airspace.

articles.title: Russia is trying to make Ukraine’s major cities uninhabitable - The Guardian
articles.body:
Russia is trying to make Ukraine’s major cities uninhabitable - The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
An intercepted document describes strikes on energy infrastructure to worsen living conditions in cities and drive an exodus of the population. The attacks have already hit facilities in the Kyiv region.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure may be part of a plan aimed at worsening living conditions in major cities and forcing the country to capitulate. The Guardian writes about this, citing a document that, according to Ukrainian intelligence, was intercepted in Russia, reports UNN.
Details
The attacks on power plants reflect a Russian plan to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable. The Kremlin is resorting to punishing the population of Ukraine in major cities, as the front lines remain frozen
According to the publication, the document titled "Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy and Housing and Utilities Sectors" contains an assessment of vulnerable facilities in Ukraine’s energy system and even anticipates strikes on high-risk facilities, in particular distribution substations at several nuclear power plants. It describes the possible consequences of the strikes—from a "deterioration in the quality of life" of Ukrainians due to power outages to a complete cessation of water supplies, which, as coldly predicted in the document, would cause "a deterioration in sanitary conditions and the forced departure of residents from cities."
According to the publication, the document does not specify which Russian agency prepared it; however, according to several European officials interviewed by the publication, the authors may have been connected to Russian military or intelligence services.
As Russian missiles and drones systematically struck power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the ongoing outages of electricity and water increasingly resemble an alleged Russian plan to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities, which the Guardian newspaper has seen. Even when Donald Trump unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" between Moscow and Kyiv last week, Russia continued its methodical and destructive strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, including in Kyiv, as part of a strategy aimed at punishing Ukraine’s population and driving the country to capitulation
According to the publication, this year "Russia appears to be putting these plans into practice."
In particular, on Tuesday evening, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region—CHP-4 and CHP-5, and the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region—as well as a major electrical substation that transmits electricity from the country’s two main nuclear power plants to the capital.
These, together with other substations forming the "Kyiv energy ring," which helps supply electricity from across the country to the capital, became targets of a Russian barrage that, if successful, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in the city of 3 million people
It should be recalled
Russia attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in 10 regions overnight and in the morning of October 17, leaving some residents without electricity. Electricity outage schedules are in effect in a number of regions.

articles.title: Bill tabled in US Congress to block deal on Russian diesel fuel
articles.body:
Bill tabled in US Congress to block deal on Russian diesel fuel
Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and Ranking Member of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at blocking the US-Russia deal on diesel fuel.
Source: the US House Foreign Affairs Committee's website
Details: The bill would prohibit the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russia's energy sector; revoke general licences issued by the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and prohibit future licences; and require US President Donald Trump's administration to impose sanctions on Russia's energy sector.
The bill has 17 co-sponsors in the House of Representatives.
Quote from Meeks: "This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for Trump's failed war of choice in Iran. It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity."
"At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cosying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine. This goes against everything the United States stands for. Congress must act. Every Member of Congress who claims to be outraged by this should join in passing this legislation."
Previously: Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Background:
- In September and October, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to scale back attacks on Russian oil refineries, linking the strikes to fuel shortages and rising prices in the US.
- On 8 October, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that talks would take place in the US involving a Ukrainian delegation. This delegation included Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People party; Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service; Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; and Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
- Ahead of the meeting, Axios reported, citing US and Ukrainian officials, that US President's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning to present "new ideas and proposals" in Miami to break the diplomatic deadlock.
- On 9 October, Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- US Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick announced that a new bipartisan bill was being prepared to block any purchases of Russian oil. Fitzpatrick's fellow Republican Don Bacon said Trump's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel looks like weakness.
- On 15 October, the Kremlin announced that Russian diesel fuel had begun reaching global markets following an agreement with Trump.

articles.title: Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade tariffs targeting Russia is a grave error that encourages Russian President Vladimir Putin to prolong the war, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky characterized the executive waiver of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 as part of an expanding pattern of economic concessions to Moscow that risks emboldening the Kremlin.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue,” Zelensky stated.
“I consider the diesel deal to be the first step. It seems to me that it is impossible to stop Putin in this way. On the contrary, he feels joy, happiness that he has such support. And still, we strongly hope, and I personally do, that the President of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops strikes on our energy, and stops this war.”
Zelensky stressed that coercing Kyiv into limiting asymmetric responses while easing economic restrictions on Moscow will not bring an end to hostilities.
“This cannot be achieved by restricting Ukraine’s responses against Russia for killing people,” Zelensky emphasized. “And certainly not by lifting sanctions.”
Bipartisan congressional action
Zelensky thanked members of the US Congress for securing the passage of the Graham Act, lamenting the White House’s decision to bypass legislation that enjoyed overwhelming bipartisan backing.
Midterms 2026: What Comes Next for the US and Europe?
“I am grateful to his [Lindsey Graham’s] friends in Congress who supported this law. It was a great victory – truly such bipartisan support for this law,” Zelensky said.
“And now the decision to cancel all of this, to block all of this, seems to me to be wrong. It definitely helps only the Russians. It definitely does not stop the war.”
The presidential remarks come 24 hours after Trump signed an executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, waiving sweeping trade duties and secondary sanctions enacted under the Graham Act just 48 hours before statutory enforcement was scheduled to commence on Sunday, Oct. 18.
The suspended provisions included an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports alongside mandatory 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, such as China and India.
The waiver also halted enforcement against third-party countries facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and suspended actions aimed at dismantling Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet” of oil tankers.
Section 115 waivers
In the executive order, Trump invoked Section 115 of the Graham Act, which authorizes the executive branch to waive statutory penalties upon certifying to Congress that such action serves US national interests. However, the administration did not provide public details regarding the strategic rationale for the determination.
The presidential waiver follows a bilateral commercial agreement unveiled on Oct. 9 between Trump and Putin, under which Moscow consented to export refined diesel fuel onto international markets through 2027 to ease consumer fuel costs ahead of the US midterm elections.
To enable the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 2027.
Ukrainian officials have warned that opening global markets to Russian refined hydrocarbons provides Moscow with vital hard-currency earnings that underwrite military operations and long-range bombardments against Ukraine’s municipal power grid.
Zelensky reiterated that durable de-escalation requires intensifying allied economic pressure and maintaining enforceable deterrence, cautioning that unilateral accommodations only incentivize further Russian aggression ahead of the winter season.

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns US’ Russia sanctions relief could reward Putin and fuel more attacks
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia could encourage the Kremlin to continue its war against Ukraine, saying he fears further concessions to Moscow.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sweeping US sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues, prompting concern in Kiev as Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure continue.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he feared the move was only the beginning of a broader relaxation of restrictions.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the ‘diesel deal’ is just the first step,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
He said he still personally hoped Trump would do everything in his power to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, but argued that limiting Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian attacks while easing pressure on Moscow would not achieve that goal.
At least two people were reported killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
Zelenskyy said the US sanctions decision came on the same day Russia attacked 15 critical power-generation facilities across Ukraine in what he described as one of the largest assaults on the country’s energy grid.
Officials said a Russian attack in the southern city of Kherson killed one person and wounded 22 others, including two children. Another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia was seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity and heating ahead of winter, when damage to energy infrastructure could have severe consequences for civilians.
Last winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Ukraine experienced prolonged interruptions to heating and electricity during freezing temperatures.
The Ukrainian president called on Kiev’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow and argued that sanctions were intended to raise the cost of continuing the war.
Kiev urges Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow
Zelenskyy also appealed to the United States to reconsider its approach to sanctions, highlighting the Lindsey Graham Act, which targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, Putin and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western restrictions.
The legislation, named after the late US senator who sponsored it, was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” Zelenskyy said on social media, arguing that the sanctions framework could still help bring the conflict to an end.
He warned that easing restrictions while Russia continued attacking Ukraine risked rewarding the aggressor and encouraging further military action.
Trump’s sanctions waiver followed his announcement of a deal with Putin allowing Russian diesel exports in exchange for sanctions relief.
The US president’s move came shortly after Putin, appearing in military uniform, said Moscow aimed to capture the remaining parts of eastern Ukraine.
Moscow welcomes Trump’s decision as talks stall
Russian officials welcomed the sanctions relief, although the Kremlin and Putin had not issued a direct response to Trump’s announcement at the time of the report.
Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, described the suspension of the Graham Act as an “important and truly historic moment”. He argued that the legislation would have caused serious damage to the US economy and global markets.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday, urging the European Union to continue financing Ukraine’s defence. He said he was standing up for his country amid the dispute with Washington.
As Russian strikes continue and winter approaches, Kiev is pressing its allies to sustain economic and military support while diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.

articles.title: Zelensky: Starlink Capped at 161 km/h, Disabling Interceptors
articles.body:
A hard speed limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph) imposed on Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine has disabled domestic interceptor drones deployed against Russian jet-powered Shahed loitering munitions, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky disclosed that satellite terminals automatically disconnect whenever equipped platforms exceed the 161 km/h threshold, causing defenders to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today our interceptors are not working because there is a speed limit,” Zelensky stated. “The maximum speed today is 161 km/h; after exceeding it, Starlink shuts down and we lose the drone.”
The Ukrainian leader stressed that Starlink remains vital for military and civilian communications across the country, highlighting its role in guiding robotic and unmanned supply runs that deliver food and potable water to frontline infantry holding isolated positions inaccessible to conventional wheeled vehicles.
However, the operational impact on airspace defense has proven severe, rendering domestic interceptors unable to engage Russian turbine-propelled loitering munitions that cruise at several hundred kilometers per hour.
Cross-border testing confirms geographical restriction
Zelensky revealed that Ukrainian technical specialists conducted comparative trials to determine whether the velocity thresholds stemmed from global technical adjustments or deliberate geographical parameters.
Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports Again
To test the system, Ukrainian authorities dispatched vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into EU territory, operating them at speeds of 180 km/h (112 mph). During the tests, the satellite links functioned normally without disconnections.
“The conclusion is as follows: the restrictions operate on the territory of Ukraine and do not operate on the territory of EU countries,” Zelensky emphasized. “That is, this is a planned operation.”
The president noted that while technical representatives across various channels describe the disconnections as engineering malfunctions, the issue remains strictly confined to Ukrainian airspace.
“At various levels they say these are technical problems,” Zelensky added. “But these technical problems exist in Ukraine; on the territory of the EU they do not exist.”
Blocked communications
Zelensky stated that Ukrainian military commanders, the Ministry of Defense, and foreign diplomats are conducting active negotiations to resolve the constraints. However, he noted that management at SpaceX has declined direct dialogue with Ukrainian military representatives.
Kyiv continues to await formal clarifications from both the Pentagon and SpaceX regarding the timeline for the restoration of unrestricted functionality across the military-grade Starshield variant, with data transfer rates remaining volatile.
The revelations follow statements delivered earlier on Saturday by US President Donald Trump, who denied involvement in service curbs, asserting that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational limits. Trump claimed to reporters that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
Trump’s statements contradict reporting published by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk proposed service caps directly to Trump, who approved the initiative, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield capabilities.
Sources indicated that Musk sought to deflect responsibility onto the White House amid concerns over consumer backlash across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.
Ukrainian officials have underscored that restricting satellite connectivity compromises baseline defensive capabilities, preventing mobile air defense teams and unmanned aviation units from shielding urban settlements and municipal power infrastructure ahead of the winter heating season.

articles.title: Russian strikes reduce Ukrainian capacity to produce long-range weapons — Gerasimov
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. As a result of 12 massive Russian strikes this fall, 30 Ukrainian defense industry companies and logistics centers have been hit, thereby significantly reducing Kiev’s ability to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, Russian Armed Forces’ General Staff Chief Army General Valery Gerasimov told President Vladimir Putin.
"In total, [Russian servicemen] carried out 12 massive strikes in September and October, striking 30 military-industrial complex enterprises and logistics centers involved in the production and storage of missiles and strike drones, as well as 14 fuel, energy, and transport infrastructure facilities. As a result, the Ukrainian industry’s capacity to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as to procure the necessary equipment to support Ukraine’s industrial and energy sectors has been significantly reduced," he said.

articles.title: Zelensky: US Preparing Proposal for Trilateral Summit
articles.body:
US officials are formulating a proposal to convene a trilateral summit between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky disclosed that Washington is actively reviewing potential venues to host direct leader-level negotiations, with potential options including the upcoming Group of 20 summit in the United States, locations across the Middle East, or a European host nation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The United States is working on this. They have a proposal for a trilateral meeting,” Zelensky said.
“This meeting could take place in one of the countries of the Middle East. The United States frequently mentions the Emirates or Saudi Arabia. Furthermore, this meeting could take place in the United States during the G20 summit.”
Zelensky noted that European governments have also initiated diplomatic outreach regarding the possibility of hosting the high-level consultations within Europe. However, the Ukrainian head of state stressed that neither the US nor the Russia has formally confirmed the summit parameters.
“There is also the option of a European country, and the Europeans have already started contacts regarding this,” Zelensky added.
“Neither the Russian side nor the American side has confirmed it yet, so we will talk about the results when there are any.”
EU Backs €70B Request as Fico Rebuffs New Loan
G20 considerations
The potential inclusion of the G20 platform aligns with recent diplomatic maneuvers surrounding the multilateral leaders’ summit scheduled to convene in Miami, Florida, this December.
Earlier on Saturday, US President Donald Trump told reporters that he remains uncertain whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Miami gathering, but affirmed that he “would love to have him” participate.
However, prospective leader-level discussions in the United States face significant diplomatic and legal complexities.
EU leadership has strongly criticized overtures inviting the Russian head of state, citing unsealed US criminal indictments against Russian intelligence operatives and an outstanding arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague charging Putin with war crimes connected to the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.
Alternative venues in the Middle East – specifically the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia – have frequently served as neutral diplomatic conduits during the conflict, facilitating bilateral prisoner-of-war exchanges and high-level backchannel discussions between Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow.
Bilateral envoy coordination
The proposal for a trilateral summit follows intensive diplomatic coordination between Kyiv and White House envoys over recent days.
Zelensky confirmed earlier on Saturday that Ukrainian negotiators, led by National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, held substantive consultations on Friday, Oct. 16, with US special diplomatic envoy Jared Kushner.
The discussions focused on establishing a timetable, venue, and working format for upcoming in-person bilateral meetings, which Kyiv expects to finalize within the coming week.
“Yesterday our negotiating group was in contact: Umerov spoke with Kushner,” Zelensky previously stated. “They are arranging a meeting, and I am also ready to meet with them. We support the possibility of dialogue – anything to stop Putin, at least in the format of an energy ceasefire.”
The outreach coincides with parallel backchannel diplomacy pursued by Washington. Russian state news agency TASS previously reported that Kushner alongside fellow US special envoy Steve Witkoff could travel to Moscow in mid-to-late October following an Oct. 9 telephone consultation between Trump and Putin.
Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to organize direct discussions, the Kremlin has maintained an unyielding diplomatic stance.
Following the Oct. 9 telephone call, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media that Putin rejected resuming formal peace negotiations, asserting that Russian forces hold the operational initiative across the front line and intend to pursue military operations until all stated objectives are fulfilled.
