articles.title: Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
articles.body:
Trump waives ‘bone-crushing’ Russia sanctions
US President Donald Trump has suspended sweeping new sanctions against Russia that he signed into law just a month ago, invoking a national-interest exemption to waive penalties targeting Moscow’s economy and countries purchasing Russian energy.
In an executive order issued on Friday, Trump waived sanctions and tariffs mandated by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, including proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
“I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification,” Trump wrote.
China and India, the two largest buyers of Russian crude oil, were expected to be among the countries hardest hit by the legislation.
The bill, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, has been described by supporters as a “bone-crushing” measure aimed at driving Russian energy exports out of the global market. Hawkish US lawmakers argued that existing restrictions had allowed Moscow to circumvent economic pressure.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. The move sparked outrage in Ukraine and among America’s European allies, prompting a bipartisan group of US senators to accuse Trump of betraying Kiev.
According to US media reports, Trump decided to ease sanctions after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which Trump blamed for high energy prices.
On Friday, US Representative Gregory Meeks introduced a bill in Congress seeking to block the diesel agreement with Russia. The Democrat accused Trump of “cozying up to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine.”
Trump has defended the agreement as beneficial to American consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda. In response to the backlash, he attacked Zelensky as “not a good guy for us to deal with” and suggested that Ukraine needed “a new president.”
Russia has maintained that it has adapted to mounting Western economic pressure, while describing the Graham bill as a hostile move that would undermine Trump’s efforts to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev.
“[Russian] diesel has begun reaching global markets, and it will have a certain positive effect on stabilizing oil markets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Thursday.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s investment envoy and a negotiator on Ukraine, hailed the waiver as “an important and historic moment.” Economic cooperation serves the interests of both countries, “contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Ukraine in Talks With Trump Envoys Over Energy Truce
articles.body:
Ukrainian officials maintain continuous communication with US President Donald Trump’s special diplomatic envoys to explore mechanisms to halt Russian military aggression, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Speaking with journalists, Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian negotiators conducted bilateral discussions with senior White House representatives on Friday, Oct. 16, to coordinate upcoming in-person meetings.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Specifically, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov held consultations with US special envoy Jared Kushner to establish a timetable and venue for comprehensive negotiations.
“Yesterday our negotiating group was in contact: Umerov spoke with Kushner,” Zelensky said. “They are arranging a meeting, and I am also ready to meet with them.”
Zelensky explained that Kyiv had anticipated convening discussions with American representatives on the sidelines of high-level European summits in Brussels earlier in the week, though that encounter did not materialize. However, the Ukrainian leader affirmed that both teams are working to finalize the format and timing of a bilateral meeting within the coming week.
“We support the possibility of dialogue – anything to stop [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, at least in the format of an energy ceasefire,” Zelensky stated. “It is preferable to end this war completely, but we must start somewhere. At the very least, meetings are necessary, and these meetings are being planned.”
Russia Hits 15 Energy Sites in Massive Strike, Zelensky Says
Diplomatic maneuvering
The diplomatic outreach arrives as Kyiv navigates complex negotiations surrounding prospective truces to shield municipal infrastructure ahead of the winter heating season.
Trump previously declared an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, asserting that both belligerents had agreed to halt strikes against power grids and petrochemical facilities.
However, implementation mechanisms have remained ambiguous, with Russian forces sustaining long-range missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian electricity generation and transmission infrastructure.
Zelensky has reiterated that Ukraine is prepared to halt asymmetric drone strikes on Russian oil refineries provided Moscow agrees to a reciprocal, verifiable cessation of strikes against Ukrainian municipal energy networks, backed by binding international guarantees.
US envoy contacts
The coordination between Umerov and Kushner follows parallel diplomatic tracks explored by Washington to initiate consultations with the Kremlin.
Earlier in the month, Russian state news agency TASS reported that Kushner alongside fellow US special envoy Steve Witkoff could visit Moscow in mid-to-late October following a telephone discussion between Trump and Putin on Oct. 9.
Following that call, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media that Putin rejected resuming formal peace negotiations, asserting that Russian forces hold the operational initiative along the front line and indicating that Moscow intends to continue hostilities until all operational objectives are met.

articles.title: Romania shoots down two drones over Black Sea
articles.body:
Romania has said it shot down two drones that entered its airspace over the Black Sea, the latest in a series of incidents believed to be spillover from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Facebook on Saturday that Romanian F-16 fighter jets intercepted and shot down both drones about 20 kilometres southeast of Sulina.
“Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country,” he wrote.
The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 local time (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes, Miruta said.
The second was downed at 18:05, five minutes after crossing into the country’s airspace.
Two F-16 fighter jets of the Romanian Air Force engaged the drones, according to a press release of the defence ministry.
NATO has previously shot down four drones in Romania's airspace, all of them this year.
Russian drone incursions
Romania, a NATO member bordering Ukraine, has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions since the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022. Much of the border follows the Danube, close to Ukrainian ports targeted by Russian forces.
The latest incident follows drone strikes on two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast earlier this week.
Romanian authorities resumed searches on Friday for seven missing sailors from one of the vessels, raising further concerns about the war’s impact on commercial shipping.
Neighbouring Bulgaria has also requested NATO combat aircraft and anti-drone systems following attacks on ships in the Black Sea. Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday that Sofia had formally sought additional support to strengthen its defences.

articles.title: Ukraine has confirmation Starlink speed restrictions apply only within its territory – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received confirmation that the speed-based restrictions on Starlink satellite communication terminals apply only within Ukraine, and he views this as a planned operation.
"What is the current speed limit for Starlink? Today, the maximum speed is 161 kilometers per hour; after that, according to the reports I have seen, Starlink shuts down completely and we lose the drone. What have we done to determine whether these are truly technical issues at SpaceX, or whether this is some kind of operation or an agreement to restrict us, shut us down, and prevent us from defending ourselves and protecting our people – both on the front lines and among civilians? We sent a couple of vehicles equipped with Starlink into European Union countries, and they drove – where permitted – at speeds exceeding 180 kilometers per hour, and Starlink worked. We have the relevant records and evidence. The conclusion is this: the restrictions apply within Ukraine, but they do not apply within the European Union. In other words, this is a planned operation," Zelenskyy said, responding to journalists' questions on Saturday.
He said a dialogue is underway with SpaceX at various levels, "and at various levels, they say these are technical issues."
"But, as I've already said, these technical issues exist in Ukraine; there are no such issues within the European Union. We've verified this. Here, Starlink works up to a speed of 161 kilometers per hour, then it shuts off. Within the EU, it works at speeds of 180 kilometers per hour and above, and it works continuously," the president said.
Zelenskyy expressed regret that "we cannot currently use Starlink or StarShield technology within our country's borders to shoot down jet-powered suicide drones." "Unfortunately, they're flying, and we can stop them with our air force; we stop them using other means, but we don't use Starlink for this, unfortunately. God willing, this work will resume," the president added.
He said Starlink is crucial for Ukraine, both on the front lines and for civilians.
"We're helping and using Starlink for drones so that we can deliver food and water to our troops in combat positions. This is very important in places where military personnel or certain types of equipment cannot reach. In areas that are cut off due to enemy drone control. And right now, we simply don't have that capability," the head of state said.
The president also said Ukraine is using Starlink on some interceptor drones to intercept high-speed enemy kamikaze drones equipped with jet engines. "Of course, and thank God, thanks to our air defense systems, our engineers, and our partners' equipment as well, we're using not only interceptor drones against kamikaze drones, but also aircraft, missiles, and other air defense systems, and so on. But again, when it comes to intercepting high-speed jet-powered drones – such as the Shahed and other jet-powered drones – our interceptors are currently ineffective because of speed limitations," Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
articles.body:
Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

articles.title: Trump rejects nuclear option against Iran, mentions ‘mother of all bombs’
articles.body:
Trump rejects nuclear option against Iran, mentions ‘mother of all bombs’
U.S. President Donald Trump has ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying the United States can achieve its military objectives without them, while leaving open the possibility of further strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports, citing Anadolu Agency.
In an interview with Newsmax, Trump was asked about reports that his administration was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iran, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump emphasized that the weapon is conventional rather than nuclear.
“The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” he said, adding that the United States had no need to use nuclear weapons.
However, the president indicated that Washington could launch additional attacks on Iran's nuclear infrastructure, specifically mentioning Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified underground site associated with Iran's nuclear programme.
“Now we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast,” Trump said in the interview.
Trump also said he did not anticipate deploying U.S. ground troops to Iran.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Trump cast doubt on Zacharia’s future as White House press secretary.

articles.title: Zelensky treating Europe as his ‘personal ATM’ – MEP
articles.body:
Zelensky treating Europe as his ‘personal ATM’ – MEP
Italian far-right MEP Roberto Vannacci has accused Vladimir Zelensky of treating Europe like an “ATM” after the Ukrainian leader requested another €70 billion ($79 billion) in aid.
Zelensky demanded more money on Friday, just months after the EU approved a massive €90 billion loan to support Ukraine through 2027. “The war will cost 155 billion euros next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros more from you – for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount,” he said at an EU summit in Brussels.
Vannacci said Italian taxpayers should not have to foot the bill for further aid to Kiev.
“Zelensky has found some suckers who give him all the billions he asks for, so he just keeps on asking for more,” the MEP said in a video on social media on Friday. He argued that Zelensky’s demands have continued to mount, citing Kiev’s alleged budget shortfalls of €27 billion in 2026 and €32 billion in 2027, followed by a fresh €70 billion demand on top of the €90 billion loan approved in April.
He’s come to view us as Ukraine’s personal ATM.
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has also rejected the proposed funding, stressing that Bratislava would not participate in another EU financial mechanism for Ukraine. Hungary has adopted a similar position, Fico said, according to Slovakia’s TASR news agency on Friday.
Slovakia, Hungary, and the Czech Republic secured exemptions from the financial obligations of the previous €90 billion loan, which EU leaders agreed late last year and finalized in April 2026. Fico has argued that the loan, which is intended to be repaid using future Russian reparations, is effectively a gift that EU members will never recover.
Moscow has long argued that Western military aid only burdens the European taxpayer and prolongs the conflict – which Russia sees as a NATO-led proxy war fought using Ukrainian manpower.

articles.title: Ukraine’s ADF down four Kalibr missiles, 289 drones in overnight Russian attack
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ADF down four Kalibr missiles, 289 drones in overnight Russian attack
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on Friday, October 16, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions and temporarily occupied Crimea; Kh-22/32 cruise missiles launched from the airspace over Crimea; four sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles launched from Novorossiysk; and 332 attack UAVs, including Shahed drones (31 of them jet-powered), S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoy drones.
The drones were launched from the directions of Oryol, Bryansk, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 on Saturday, October 17, air defenses had shot down or suppressed 293 targets: four Kalibr cruise missiles; 289 UAVs, including Shahed drones (23 of them jet-powered), S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones and drones of other types.
Hits were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, air raid alerts were issued in Kyiv and several other regions in the morning of October 17 due to a ballistic missile threat. The Air Force warned of missile launches targeting Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih.

articles.title: Iran’s missile capabilities have changed the equation, caretaker defense minister warns US
articles.body:
Iran’s missile capabilities have changed the equation, caretaker defense minister warns US
TEHRAN- Iran’s caretaker Defense Minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza, has responded to US President Donald Trump’s threats against Iran, warning that any renewed military action would carry consequences for Washington’s international standing, economy and domestic political calculations.
In a post on X, Ebn al-Reza dismissed speculation about the possible use of the US military’s most powerful conventional bomb against Iran, stressing that the size and name of a weapon would not determine the outcome of a confrontation.
“The names and dimensions of bombs do not matter!” he wrote.
“Your bombs will explode somewhere else: in your global standing, the US economy, and even your electoral calculations!” he added.
The Iranian general said the country’s missile capabilities had fundamentally altered the strategic equation, telling US officials that Washington would have to adjust to a new reality.
“It is our missile power that has changed the equations and brought you to the point where, from now on, you must say: ‘Yes, sir!’” he wrote.
Ebn al-Reza’s remarks came amid reports that the US military had considered additional strike options involving the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “Mother of All Bombs.” The weapon is one of the largest conventional bombs in the US arsenal.
Reports have raised the possibility of further attacks on Iranian infrastructure and nuclear-related facilities should Trump order a resumption of military operations. However, the existence of military options does not necessarily mean that a decision to carry them out has been made.
The deliberations have also renewed questions about the military and economic consequences of escalating the conflict, including whether additional bombing could achieve Washington’s objectives without triggering wider regional repercussions.
Iran’s defense chief framed the country’s missile capabilities as a central factor in the strategic calculations facing the United States. His message was that the destructive power of individual weapons cannot, on its own, determine the outcome of a conflict.
The warning also extended beyond the battlefield. By highlighting the potential effects on the US economy, international standing, and electoral calculations, Ebn al-Reza pointed to the wider costs that a renewed confrontation could impose on Washington.

articles.title: Liberation of DPR, security zone, continuation of massive strikes: Putin’s statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia will continue launching strikes against Ukrainian defense enterprises and logistics centers, Russian President Vladimir Putin said while visiting an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force.
He stressed that the establishment of a buffer zone will not be open to discussion with Kiev and thanked Russian troops fighting to liberate Dobropolye and Alexeyevo-Drushkovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR).
TASS has compiled the president’s key statements.
Russia’s objectives
After Ukraine’s incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region, Russian forces were tasked not only with driving the enemy out of Russian territory but also with establishing a security zone, and this task is being successfully implemented: "Our task is to ensure absolute security of Russia’s border territories in the future and we are not going to make this a subject of any potential peace talks with Ukraine."
Commanders of battlegroups must continue "carrying out tasks in strict compliance with the objectives of the special military operation." "Naturally, it is necessary to continue massive and coordinated strikes against enemy defense facilities and logistics centers."
Strikes against the Kiev regime’s facilities have been effective: "I assess the results positively."
"As for the situation on the ground, naturally, one of the key objectives is the liberation of the Donetsk People’s Republic."
Successes
Russian forces are advancing along the entire frontline in the zone of the special military operation, and "the pace of their advance has increased significantly."
Russia’s armed forces continue to carry out the objectives of the special military operation: "As has already been mentioned here, in September alone, more than 1,300 square kilometers of territory in Donbas and Novorossiya was liberated."
"Around 6,500 square kilometers of territory and 310 settlements have been liberated since the beginning of this year."
The liberation of Dobropolye in the DPR is an evident success: "Please convey my words of gratitude to all personnel directly involved in the liberation of Dobropolye. I will say more about this when addressing the commanders of the task forces, but I want to emphasize and point out right here: the capture of Dobropolye is undoubtedly a significant milestone in the liberation of Donbas as a whole and a clear success for the Russian Armed Forces. Congratulations to you all."
"The enemy had turned the city into a fortified stronghold in this area, but the coordinated and highly professional actions of Russian assault units made it possible first to encircle enemy forces in the city and then to take complete control of it."
The liberation of Dobropolye "opens a direct route toward the DPR’s borders."
The liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka and the start of the assault on Ukrainian fortified areas in Druzhkovka and Kramatorsk in the DPR create conditions for "the swiftest possible completion of the liberation of Donbas from the Kiev regime’s combat units."
"Please convey my most sincere words of gratitude to all the personnel who were directly involved in the liberation of Alexeyevo-Druzhkovka for the courage and resilience they demonstrated during this combat operation."
Russian forces successfully encircled a Ukrainian grouping 2,000 troops in the Kharkov Region: "Entrapping a grouping of about 2,000 troops, in an area of more than 400 square kilometers, 460 square kilometers, is certainly no ordinary feat. Taking into account the subsequent elimination of the enemy in that area, this is indeed a success."
"The offensive in the Zaporozhye Region continues at a high pace, with Battlegroups Dnepr and East’s troops advancing successfully."
"A decisive role [in ensuring rapid progress] undoubtedly belongs to our soldiers and officers, who, while carrying out combat missions, act professionally and demonstrate the finest qualities of the Russian military, such as selfless devotion to the Motherland."
Protection of facilities
Air defense combat crews are operating professionally: "But, of course, there is room for improvement in this regard. We need to enhance the effectiveness of our defense of civilian, first and foremost civilian, and, of course, military facilities."

articles.title: Hypersonic-armed stealth destroyer nears sea trials
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy added $99.1 million to an Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover sea trials for USS Lyndon B. Johnson, the last Zumwalt-class destroyer.
- The ship is being fitted in Pascagoula with Conventional Prompt Strike hypersonic missiles, following USS Zumwalt, which finished sea trials in January 2026.
The U.S. Navy is paying Huntington Ingalls Industries another $99.1 million to take USS Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG 1002), the last of its three angular Zumwalt-class stealth destroyers, through sea trials as the ship is fitted to carry hypersonic missiles.
The contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, raises the ceiling on an existing Ingalls Shipbuilding contract to cover the destroyer’s sea trials. About 95% of the work will take place at the company’s shipyard in Pascagoula, Mississippi, with completion scheduled for October 2028, and the U.S. Navy obligated about $59.3 million at signing, split between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds.
During sea trials, a new or heavily modified warship leaves the yard to run its propulsion, steering, combat systems and other equipment at sea before the U.S. Navy accepts it. For Lyndon B. Johnson, they will follow years of work in Pascagoula to turn the ship into one of the first U.S. warships able to fire Conventional Prompt Strike, a hypersonic missile designed to reach targets thousands of kilometers away at more than five times the speed of sound.
The Zumwalt class was originally designed around two 155 mm Advanced Gun Systems meant to bombard targets ashore, but the U.S. Navy canceled the guns’ special long-range shells in 2016 after costs soared, leaving the destroyers with guns they could not use, and later decided to remove them and give the three ships a new strike mission with hypersonic missiles.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works in Maine built Lyndon B. Johnson, which was christened in April 2019 by the late president’s daughters, before moving to Ingalls for combat system activation. In January 2025 the ship entered dry dock in Pascagoula to start installing the large missile tubes for Conventional Prompt Strike, and the U.S. Navy said at the time that it planned to commission the destroyer in 2027.
The lead ship, USS Zumwalt (DDG 1000), went through the same conversion first. Ingalls replaced its forward gun with four large-diameter tubes that each hold three hypersonic missiles, giving the ship 12 in total, and Zumwalt completed builder’s sea trials in January 2026 after nearly three years in the yard, HII said. The second ship, USS Michael Monsoor (DDG 1001), is set to receive the same missile system during a future yard period.
Conventional Prompt Strike shares its hypersonic glide body with the U.S. Army’s Dark Eagle long-range hypersonic weapon, which the U.S. Army fields on truck-mounted launchers. The missile boosts its warhead to high speed and altitude, then releases a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward the target, making it harder for air and missile defenses to intercept. Lockheed Martin, the program’s prime contractor, received a $1.36 billion contract modification earlier this year to support missile and launcher production for the system.
Ingalls is due to finish Lyndon B. Johnson’s sea trials and related work by October 2028, which would make it the second Zumwalt-class destroyer to go to sea with hypersonic missile tubes.

articles.title: Ukraine was not warned about the suspension of U.S. sanctions against Russia — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine was not warned about the suspension of U.S. sanctions against Russia — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
The president said that Ukraine had not been warned about the suspension of the sanctions. Due to Starlink's technical restrictions, the state is losing drones and communications.
Ukraine did not receive any warnings about the suspension of U.S. sanctions. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this while speaking with journalists. He also reported that Ukraine continues negotiations concerning the operation of Starlink and Starshield, UNN reports.
Details
No, we did not receive any warning that the sanctions would be suspended overnight. Just as we knew nothing about the Diesel Deal, and just as we learned about the possibility of an energy truce from the media. So, as of today, that is the situation. As for Starlink and Starshield: yes, we are engaged in dialogue, at the military level, at the level of the Ministry of Defense, and at the diplomatic level; we are contacting everyone, including SpaceX. However, no one is currently responding to our military personnel or the Ministry of Defense. At various levels, they say that these are technical problems
Zelenskyy reported that because of the Starlink outages, Ukraine is losing drones and communications.
But, as I have already said, these technical problems exist in Ukraine. There are no such problems in the territory of the European Union. We checked this. Our Starlink works at speeds of up to 161 km/h, and then it shuts down. In the EU, it works at 180-plus and operates continuously. Here, it shuts down after 161 km/h for the second minute, switches off, and stops working. We are undoubtedly losing both drones and communications. Unfortunately, today we cannot use Starlink or Starshield technology in our country to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. Unfortunately, they are flying, and we can stop them with aircraft; we stop them using other means and other air-defense systems, but unfortunately, we do not use Starlink for this. God willing, this work will be restored
Reminder
Earlier, the media reported that Volodymyr Zelenskyy had allegedly agreed to a 100-day pause in strikes on Russia's energy infrastructure in exchange for an expansion of Starlink. He is also considering Patriot missiles.

articles.title: Russian night attacks on Ukrainian regions: one person killed in Kherson, dozens injured, and infrastructure damaged
articles.body:
Russian night attacks on Ukrainian regions: one person killed in Kherson, dozens injured, and infrastructure damaged
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked a number of regions in Ukraine with missiles, aircraft, and drones. An ambulance driver was killed, and dozens of people, including children, were injured.
During the night of October 17 and in the morning, Russian forces carried out a series of missile, air, and drone attacks on Ukrainian regions. Kharkiv, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Sumy region, and other regions came under attack. One person was reported killed, dozens injured, including children, and residential buildings and industrial facilities were damaged. This was reported by local military administrations, police, and rescuers, UNN writes.
Details
In Kherson, Russian aircraft attacked the Korabelnyi district on the morning of October 17. According to Yarоslav Shanko, head of the city military administration, a 64-year-old ambulance driver was killed. Among those injured were an 11-year-old girl and a family with a one-month-old infant. A paramedic was also injured during a repeated strike.
In Zaporizhzhia, the Russians struck a residential area. According to the regional military administration, five people, including a child, were injured. Apartment buildings were damaged, and cars caught fire as a result of the attack.
Mass strikes on Kharkiv, Sumy region, and the central regions
In Kharkiv, 15 people, including three children, were injured as a result of a missile attack on the evening of October 16. One of the strikes hit a warehouse building in the Nemyshlianskyi district, where a fire covering an area of 100 square meters broke out. Nearby high-rise buildings were damaged, and rescuers extinguished four fires.
In the Sumy region, 25 Russian shelling attacks were recorded over the course of the day, with 19 settlements coming under fire. According to the police, eight people were injured. In the Sumy community, six residents sustained injuries and trauma, while another woman suffered an acute stress reaction. In the Znob-Novhorodske community, a 52-year-old woman was injured as a result of a drone strike.
In Kryvyi Rih, Russian forces attacked an industrial enterprise. In Dnipro, according to local authorities, a combined attack involving ballistic and cruise missiles was recorded. Explosions were also reported in Zhytomyr and the Chernivtsi region.
Explosions were also heard in the Khmelnytskyi region, where widespread power outages were reported in the northern part of the region. Meanwhile, in the Cherkasy region, air defense forces neutralized six Russian drones during October 16–17. Information about the consequences of the attacks in certain regions is still being clarified.

articles.title: Britain puts stealth fighters to sea in the High North
articles.body:
British F-35 jets will fly from HMS Prince of Wales in the Arctic and North Atlantic when the carrier sails from Portsmouth on Sunday, returning fifth-generation airpower to the skies of the High North as part of the second phase of Operation Firecrest, according to the Royal Navy.
The carrier deploys with an air group comprising F-35 jets, Merlin Mk4 Commando and Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters, Wildcat helicopters and Malloy drones, accompanied by the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless and more than 1,200 British personnel.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, placed the air wing at the centre of the message: “The deployment of the HMS Prince of Wales and her air wing to the High North and the North Atlantic, operating under NATO leadership, is a clear demonstration of the UK’s commitment to the Alliance and contribution to the enduring security and stability of the North Atlantic.”
Commodore Richard Hewitt, who commands the UK Carrier Strike Group staff, said the group would work with allies throughout: “Led by the UK Flagship HMS Prince of Wales, the Strike Group will bring together a range of assets and capabilities, while taking every opportunity to train, operate and integrate with our NATO allies and partners.”
They are flown by a joint Royal Navy and Royal Air Force force based at Marham.
Operating them in the Arctic brings problems the Indo-Pacific deployment did not. Deck icing, salt spray freezing on surfaces, low cloud, short daylight and a sea state that moves the landing spot all bear on an aircraft that lands vertically onto a moving deck, and the maintainers work on an exposed flight deck in conditions that degrade both people and equipment faster than warm water does. Running a fifth-generation aircraft in that environment, and proving the stealth coatings, the sensors and the logistics chain can take it, is a large part of why the deployment is worth doing.
Russia’s Northern Fleet operates from the Kola Peninsula and the government’s Arctic Policy Framework, published this week, described it as capable of threatening Britain, Western Europe and North America, with expanded patrols and new capabilities across multiple domains. The same document committed Britain to stepping up its defence contribution in the region, including doubling the number of troops deployed to Norway to two thousand over the next three years and taking on a role in NATO air policing from Iceland.
The strike group will operate under NATO command and contribute to the alliance’s Neptune Strike series of exercises, working with Norway, Denmark and Germany. The Royal Navy said the focus of the phase is operational readiness, interoperability and preparedness to respond in a region it calls increasingly important.
Prince of Wales will also host the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo during the deployment, bringing defence leaders, industry and policymakers aboard to discuss Euro-Atlantic security.
The ship is due to leave Portsmouth Naval Base at 1700 on Sunday 18 October, weather permitting.

The enterprise designs and manufactures unmanned aerial systems used extensively by Russian forces along active combat sectors. Ukrainian defense planners noted that degrading the company’s physical infrastructure is engineered to disrupt serial assembly lines and restrict drone deliveries to frontline Russian formations.
“Damage was confirmed on Oct. 16 to the production and warehouse building of the Roboavia enterprise in the area of Khutor Lenina, Rostov region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.

Severing tactical logistics and missile brigade depot storage limits the combat readiness of Russian ground-based missile units, impeding their ability to transport, store, and maintain specialized missile armaments.
The verified strike in Latyshi follows a sequence of precision interdiction actions carried out by Ukrainian units against military transport and sustainment networks across the Bryansk border region.
Coordinated campaign against Russian logistics

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian Rail Bridge, Ammunition Warehouses
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces have struck a strategic railway bridge inside Russia’s Bryansk region, alongside multiple military logistics depots and a drone command post across occupied Donetsk region.
According to an official dispatch released by the General Staff, precision strikes were conducted throughout Friday, Oct. 16, and overnight into Saturday morning, targeting logistical nodes that sustain Russian military formations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Inside Russia, Ukrainian fire engaged a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near the settlement of Sloboda-Seletska in the Bryansk region.
Ukrainian defense planners noted that severing or degrading the crossing is engineered to disrupt Russian military rail transport, specifically interdicting shipments of ammunition, petroleum products, and heavy combat vehicles toward frontline formations.
“Damage was recorded to a railway bridge across the Unecha River in the area of Sloboda-Seletska, Bryansk region of the Russian Federation,” the General Staff announced.
“This will complicate rail logistics for Russian forces, in particular the supply of ammunition, fuel, and military equipment.”
Depots and drone control posts hit in occupied Donetsk region
Simultaneously, Ukrainian precision units targeted rear logistics hubs and unmanned aviation command installations across Russian-occupied sectors of the Donetsk region.
Military authorities confirmed direct impacts on Russian material and technical supply warehouses in the areas of Novoandriivka, Mykilske, and the port city of Mariupol.
Zelensky: ‘Putin’s Real Enemy Is the Rules-Based Order’ – Key Takeaways From Brussels
The destruction of concentrated storage depots restricts frontline Russian tactical groups from rapidly replenishing ammunition, vehicular parts, and fuel reserves along contested southern and eastern sectors.
In the vicinity of Malynivka in the Donetsk region, Ukrainian fire struck an active Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command and control post, suppressing enemy drone reconnaissance and strike coordination.
The General Staff emphasized that systematic interdiction of transport arteries, supply bases, and drone command centers forms part of a sustained campaign to degrade the combat potential and logistical stamina of Russian forces.
Asymmetric interdiction of supply corridors
The strikes across the Bryansk and Donetsk regions follow an expanding Ukrainian operational effort to dismantle critical transport bridges and chokepoints linking Russian staging bases with occupied Ukrainian territory.
In late September, Ukrainian strikes damaged the Chonhar road bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russian-held sectors of the Kherson region. Independent open-source satellite intelligence published by Dnipro OSINT showed that consecutive precision strikes blasted large craters into the roadway before causing a full bridge span to collapse by Sept. 30.
The collapse of the Chonhar span severely constrained Russian vehicular transport between the Crimean peninsula and occupied southern Ukraine, forcing Russian military logistics units onto longer, more vulnerable detours along the Sea of Azov coastal corridor.

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine still unable to use interceptors due to Starlink limits, in touch with US
articles.body:
The Ukrainian military was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions placed on services provided by satellite company Starlink, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Saturday.
"Today, our interceptor drones are not operating because of speed limitations," Zelensky said.
He said Ukraine had been told that the speed restrictions had been caused by technical issues but that tests of Starlink on the territory of the European Union had shown there were no such issues there.
US President Donald Trump said on Friday he did not think either he or Elon Musk - whose company SpaceX developed the Starshield system used by Ukraine's military - was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia.
The reduction in services provided by the satellite company interrupted communications with headquarters and caused internet speeds to drop.
Ukraine, US peace negotiators could meet next week, Zelenskiy says
Zelensky also said that Ukraine, the US, and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US, but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting, and other venues are also possible.
The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.
"The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat.
He added: "This meeting could take place in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The United States has consistently mentioned the United Arab Emirates or Saudi Arabia."
Zelensky said Ukrainian negotiators had spoken to US officials on Friday but gave no other details. He also said that Europe needed its own track for talks with Russia, with which relations are strained by Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Trump has declined to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the more than four-year-old war, and Zelensky has criticized Trump for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

articles.title: Sisi urges parliament to approve military help for Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt's Sisi seeks parliamentary approval for military support for Saudi Arabia
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday called for an emergency session of the House of Representatives to grant him authorisation to intervene in Saudi Arabia’s defence, should Riyadh request it.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony for new classes at the Egyptian Military Academy in the New Administrative Capital, Sisi explained that such a move would require parliamentary approval.
"I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to grant us authorisation to take action to intervene in defense of Saudi Arabia if we are asked to do so," the president said.
Sisi stressed that Cairo was not seeking to attack anyone or enter a war, but rather to defend Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states, without disclosing details about the nature, scope, or timing of any potential intervention.
The move comes as Yemen's Houthis have ramped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including the targeting of an Aramco building, airports, and other key infrastructure.
Article 152 of the Egyptian Constitution stipulates that the president, as Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, may neither declare war nor dispatch the armed forces on a combat mission outside the country’s borders without first consulting the National Defence Council and obtaining approval from the House of Representatives by a two-thirds majority of its members.
His statements come two days after he said, during a meeting with officials and media figures following a graduation ceremony at the Police Academy on Thursday, that Saudi Arabia’s security was directly linked to Egyptian and Arab national security. He stressed that Cairo rejected any threat to the kingdom’s security or borders, as well as any threat to maritime navigation in the Red Sea.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty previously said in an interview with Bloomberg on the sidelines of International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok that Egypt would respond to any Saudi request and was prepared to provide various forms of support, including military assistance.
He also noted that Cairo was seriously considering joining the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
At the same time, Cairo has maintained its diplomatic approach. During a phone call with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, last Tuesday, Abdelatty stressed the need for an immediate halt to attacks targeting Saudi territory, describing them as unjustified and unacceptable. He called for de-escalation and for political and diplomatic solutions to take precedence.
Sisi's latest remarks on the conflict between the Houthis and Riyadh come amid an escalation in attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, including missile and drone strikes that hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and resulted in fatalities and hundreds of injuries.

articles.title: Drone Attack Paralyzes Moscow Airports Again
articles.body:
A major wave of Ukrainian strike drones targeted the Moscow region and multiple regions early Saturday morning, Oct. 17, forcing civil aviation authorities to shut down airspace across the Russian capital and divert international flights to alternative hubs.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defense units intercepted 75 unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) heading toward the metropolitan capital. Sobyanin stated that municipal emergency services and defense specialists deployed to the sites of falling debris, without specifying the intended targets of the drone strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aerial incursions prompted Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, to enact emergency ground stops and flight restrictions across Moscow’s primary airport cluster shortly before midnight.
Among the disrupted commercial flights was a Pegasus Airlines flight transiting from Antalya, Turkey, to Moscow. Passengers reported departing Turkey at 7:35 p.m., only to be informed prior to descent that the airspace above Moscow had been sealed.
The airliner diverted to Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg, landing at approximately 1:00 a.m. local time, where passengers were instructed to remain on board until Moscow airspace reopened.
Similar flight restrictions and ground delays were instituted across regional air hubs in western Russia as air raid warnings sounded.
Ministry claims 610 drones intercepted across 15 regions
According to an operational bulletin issued by the Russian Ministry of Defense, Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 610 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones across the country between Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Meeks Introduces Bill to Block Trump-Putin Diesel Deal
The ministry claimed the overnight wave engaged targets across a broad geographical footprint spanning 15 administrative regions alongside occupied territories.
Regions targeted included the Moscow region, Leningrad, Novgorod, Tver, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Oryol, Kaluga, Voronezh, Rostov, Smolensk, and Tula regions, as well as the Krasnodar region, the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug in western Siberia, and occupied Crimea.
Compounding disruptions to Russian civil aviation
The Saturday morning aviation shutdown marks the third time in ten days that drone alerts paralyzed Moscow’s airspace.
Overnight into Friday, Oct. 16, Moscow’s four primary airports – Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky – suspended all inbound and outbound flights, forcing more than 20 commercial airliners to divert to alternate airports and causing over 200 flight cancellations before restrictions were lifted around 5:45 a.m. local time.
That disruption followed an earlier overnight shutdown on Oct. 13–14, during which more than 500 flights were delayed or canceled across the capital’s hubs.
Civil aviation data released by Rosaviatsiya head Dmitry Yadrov indicates that recurring airspace closures and drone threats have contracted commercial passenger traffic, with Russian carriers transporting 39.5 million passengers between May and August – a 7 percent decline compared to 42.6 million passengers carried during the corresponding period in 2025.
Ukrainian officials have stated that interdiction operations do not target civilian aircraft, but aim to constrain military transport and highlight the risks of utilizing Russian sovereign airspace during wartime.
In September, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned international air carriers and insurers of escalating hazards across Russian skies, stating that active airfields and logistics nodes supporting Moscow’s war effort remain valid operational targets.

Kyiv • UNN
Andrius Kubilius, the European Commissioner for Defence and Space, highlighted the importance of Fire Point’s developments.
The production of ballistic missiles by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and work on the European Freyja anti-ballistic system could bring about a huge change in the war and strengthen Europe’s defense. European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius stated this, UNN writes.
Details
So, fortunately for Europe and for Ukraine itself, we have Fire Point, which, as you know, is preparing to begin production of both ballistic missiles and Freyja anti-ballistic systems. And this could become a huge change
We remind you
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the first combat use of the FP-7, developed by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. The launch site and target were not disclosed, but it is known that the missile has a range of approximately 250 km and a warhead weighing about 200 kg. The company is also working in parallel on the FP-9, which will have a longer range and be capable of striking Moscow.
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European anti-ballistic system, the first track of the Anti-Ballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to ensure the interception of Russian ballistic missiles. The project is being built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point; other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point’s General and Technical Director Iryna Terekh said that development had reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem — radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center — while tests are being conducted up to twice a week.

articles.title: Tusk Warns Russia May Escalate Hybrid Attacks Before Christmas
articles.body:
Russia could be preparing to escalate its hybrid attacks against Poland “before Christmas Eve,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has warned.

Large-scale provocations

Polish military to practise deploying forces in Ukraine in event of ceasefire with Russia – The Times
According to The Times, 1,500 European troops will practise deploying forces to Ukraine in Poland in November in preparation for a possible ceasefire with Russia.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Times
Details: The exercises are said to be the first of their kind. They will focus on preparing for the post-war situation, in which the presence of European troops on Ukrainian territory would serve as a deterrent.
Soldiers from several countries, including France and Germany, will practise troop movements and logistical support as part of a multinational peacekeeping operation.
The publication learned that at least 1,500 British, French and German troops, along with the Polish Armed Forces, will take part in the exercises.
A source in the UK Ministry of Defence said that troops would rehearse a scenario in which "multinational forces are together in a particular area", but declined to provide further details.
A senior Polish official said the exercises would underscore the unity of Europe's major military powers in the face of the Russian threat and the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
UK Defence Secretary John Healey said in Washington that next month, "thousands of troops will take part in major exercises in Poland to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war reconstruction that Ukraine will need".
He made the remarks following his first in-person meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon.
Background:
- The exercises were agreed upon at a summit in Paris in July and announced by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
- The Coalition of the Willing, led by France and the UK, is working on a plan to deploy a mission to Ukraine to guarantee a future ceasefire.

articles.title: EU vows satellite support for Ukraine but cannot yet replace Starlink
articles.body:
The European Union has pledged to help Ukraine reduce its dependence on US-owned satellite communications, while acknowledging that it cannot replace Starlink in the short term.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said services were still being restored after disruptions he described as “a very unpleasant and dangerous surprise”.
Ukraine reported restrictions this week on some Starlink internet terminals, saying they had hampered its ability to defend against Russian forces.
The disruption came amid renewed tensions between Kiev and Washington even as US President Donald Trump denied ordering temporary disruption of Starlink service for Ukraine’s military.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy but acknowledged limits to the support Europe could immediately provide.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after the talks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Europe had no readily available replacement.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said.
Europe’s satellite plans
EU countries currently pool and share satellite communications capacity through GOVSATCOM, a programme in which the bloc wants to fully include Ukraine, EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
The EU also plans to incorporate commercial services into GOVSATCOM early next year to help meet military needs while it develops its own satellite network.
That network, known as IRIS², is intended to rival Starlink. Launches are planned for 2029, with full operations targeted for 2030.
Ukraine uses SpaceX’s military satellite service, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-controlled territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses the company’s civilian Starlink system, though not for offensive operations.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk, whose stance on Ukraine has shifted repeatedly since 2022, said this week that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
Limited alternatives
European support extends beyond EU programmes. France’s Eutelsat already provides satellite communications services to Ukraine through its OneWeb network, although it has disclosed little about government and military uses.
Its constellation of 648 satellites, however, is far smaller than Starlink’s network of more than 10,000.
According to specialist publication Via Satellite, OneWeb cannot support drone and ground robot operations because of limited capacity and a lack of compact satellite terminals.
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked, stressing that those gaps needed to be filled “as soon as possible”.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also underscored Ukraine’s dependence on the service.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine, actually, to fight or fight back,” he told reporters. “It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have it, but not enough.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed Starlink with Macron on Thursday, including how European countries could provide more such services in the near future.

articles.title: How one invented claim becomes a chatbot’s confident answer in cognitive warfare: Ukraine’s drone chief maps Russia’s AI attack
articles.body:
Ask a chatbot why something happened in the war, and the answer may be written by Russia. Russia is poisoning AI chatbots with millions of fake articles so they repeat Kremlin narratives as fact, a cognitive weapon with strategic impact, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madiar” Brovdi warns on Telegram.
Russia has waged a cognitive war against Ukraine for years, and it intensified sharply with the full-scale invasion. This war goes beyond fake news and disinformation: it aims to shape the deeply ingrained beliefs that drive people’s attitudes, decisions and behavior, and its newest weapon is artificial intelligence.
Brovdi calls it a cognitive operation with strategic impact, one his forces studied among the technological risks of 2027. People increasingly ask a chatbot “why did X happen?” and take the instant answer, he explains, without asking where it comes from.
“Artificial intelligence does not know the truth. It retells the internet, literally,” Brovdi claims.
How the strategy works, step by step
Brovdi lays out a chain that turns a single lie into something a machine will repeat as fact:
- The enemy invents a lie. For example, that Ukrainian soldiers did something terrible, when nothing of the sort happened.
- It is copied across thousands of sites. The same fabrication is published again and again, in many languages, until it looks like everyone is reporting it.
- It fakes a crowd of independent sources. The sites cross-link to one another, but ten sites copying one lie are not ten independent confirmations.
- A person asks the AI. They type “why did Ukrainian soldiers do X?”, though X may never have happened, so the lie is already smuggled into the question as fact.
- The AI may repeat the lie. If the system ingests unreliable material and checks facts poorly, it echoes the fabrication in a calm, confident tone.
- The person trusts it. “The AI said so,” they think, so the answer feels objective, and they believe it, retell it, or share it online.
- The lie shapes decisions and trust. People start to distrust the army, the state, or one another, and even an unproven fabrication has already changed how they feel.
The machines already repeat the lie
The attack runs on volume. Russia floods the web through the “Pravda” network, close to 200 sites in dozens of languages posting 4 to 6 million near-identical articles a year, Brovdi claims, written for machines, not people.
It works, by his account. Of the ten most popular chatbots studied, about a third of the time they reproduce Russian fakes, he noted, and four of ten in a 2024 test affirmed that Azov fighters had burned an effigy of Trump, a fabrication, and cited sources for it.
A war Ukraine admits it is losing
Brovdi is blunt about the balance. Ukraine is losing this fight to Russia’s troll farms, he concedes, even as a layer of homegrown trolls has sprung up too.
His closing advice was aimed at readers.
“Critical thinking should not be delegated. Not even to the smartest machine. Switch on your own judgment and always check the source and the information,” Brovdi states.

articles.title: Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
articles.body:
Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow has exposed divisions within the West over its anti-Russian stance, as the US shifts toward a more pragmatic approach, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl has said.
US President Donald Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, easing sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April 2027 in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. The move marks a departure from the Western sanctions policy imposed on Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
Speaking to TASS on Friday, Kneissl described the agreement as more than a “symbolic breakthrough,” pointing to the 300,000 tons of Russian diesel expected to reach the US and global markets by November.
“The EU says that this undermines the West’s united position. However, one could also say that this marks a shift by the US toward a more pragmatic approach, while the EU continues to pursue a purely ideological line,” she stated.
The agreement has drawn criticism from European leaders attending a two-day EU summit in Brussels this week. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused Trump of sidelining the bloc, telling reporters that “Trump, by doing that business with Putin, stabbed us in the back. We have to do something.”
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, however, welcomed the agreement, arguing that lower fuel prices were essential to Europe’s economic competitiveness. “Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate,” he said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the agreement as a “gift to Putin,” while defending Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed on Friday that the bloc would maintain its sanctions against Moscow despite Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
Brussels’ hardline stance contrasts with that of EU member Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian energy and has sought to maintain economic ties with Moscow. Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly called for diplomacy rather than continued military support for Kiev.
The dispute has also strained relations between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Vladimir Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for pushing up global fuel prices.
Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as a “weak decision” and accused Trump of “betrayal.” Ukraine continued targeting Russian energy facilities, including a refinery in Ryazan Region on Thursday, prompting Trump to condemn the attacks as a “disgrace.” At Friday’s summit, Zelensky sought additional financial and military assistance from European leaders but left empty-handed, with only renewed promises of support.
The confrontation comes as global diesel supplies remain under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, in an effort to ease shortages and bring down prices.

articles.title: War on Iran has cost EU more than $112 billion, Spanish PM Sánchez says
articles.body:
War on Iran has cost EU more than $112 billion, Spanish PM Sánchez says
TEHRAN- Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned that the war against Iran has cost Europeans more than €100 billion ($112 billion), arguing that ordinary citizens are paying the price for a conflict they opposed.
In a post on X on Friday, Sánchez said those who had spoken out against the war had been right to warn of its consequences.
“Those of us who raised our voices against the war were right when we said NO to war,” he wrote. “We knew ordinary people would end up paying the bill.”
“Now, it's time to put an end to this disaster,” Sánchez said.
His remarks underscore mounting concerns in Europe over the economic fallout of the war, particularly its effects on energy costs, household budgets and business competitiveness.
European citizens face the economic fallout
The €100 billion figure cited by Sánchez highlights the scale of the economic burden that the conflict has placed on Europe. Higher energy costs can feed through to transport, manufacturing, food prices and household expenditure, placing additional pressure on governments already grappling with economic challenges.
The economic repercussions raise a broader question for European governments: how can they protect their populations from the consequences of a conflict while addressing the extent to which their own military infrastructure has supported US operations?
British base used by US bombers in strikes on Iran
The debate has gained a further dimension following reports by major Western media outlets that US long-range bombers operating from RAF Fairford in England were used in strikes against Iran.
The Washington Post reported on October 6 that the Pentagon abruptly moved approximately a dozen B-1 bombers out of the British base amid concerns about a possible attack on the aircraft and personnel. The newspaper noted that the aircraft had recently been used in bombing missions against Iran.
Reuters also reported on October 5 that US President Donald Trump had linked the bombers' withdrawal to a security threat. The aircraft were subsequently returned to their home bases in the United States.
The episode highlights the strategic importance of European military facilities to Washington's ability to deploy and sustain long-range air operations. It also brings into focus the role of host countries in determining whether their territory and infrastructure can be used in military action against another state.
Britain had authorized the United States to use RAF Fairford for what its government described as specific and limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile sites, according to reporting by The Washington Post. Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the decision.
The distinction between the stated scope of the authorization and the broader military consequences of providing a launch platform for attacks on Iran is central to the debate over European responsibility.
A divide between opposition to war and military cooperation
Sánchez's remarks reflect the position of a European leader who has publicly opposed the war and emphasized its cost to ordinary people. The use of British territory for US bombing operations, meanwhile, illustrates that European responses to the conflict have not been uniform.
This distinction matters because opposition to a war's economic consequences is not the same as withholding military assistance that could facilitate it. Where governments permit foreign forces to use their territory for attacks, their decisions become part of the wider strategic context of the conflict.
For Iran, the issue also raises questions about the obligations of states not to allow their territory to be used in ways that facilitate unlawful uses of force.
The financial consequences identified by Sánchez and the military role of facilities such as RAF Fairford therefore point to two interconnected dimensions of the war: the costs borne by European societies and the contribution that some European infrastructure has made to US operations.
As European households and businesses contend with the economic fallout, Sánchez's call to end the conflict places renewed emphasis on the need for a political settlement that prevents further destruction and limits the war's wider regional and international consequences.

articles.title: How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
articles.body:
How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.
In messages that appear to be directed at the American public, Iran has been highlighting the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against the country ahead of the United States midterm elections.
Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets stressing the disastrous impact of the war on oil prices and the US economy, while Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has actively targeted US officials about rising costs and military spending.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Tehran is looking to increase the political cost of the war for Trump by trying to talk directly to the American public.
“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.
Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas.
On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.
The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.
“Let’s ‘play the percentages’. Not in odds, but in the % increases,” Ghalibaf wrote in a message to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading the sanctions campaign against Iran.
Bessent said last month that he represents “the house”, likening the economy to a casino while addressing the national debt and bond market.
Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.
Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.
Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.
Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.
The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.
In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.
“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. Soon, the dam will break, and the economy will implode, causing, unfortunately, great pain for Americans for many many years,” the IRGC said.
“Americans need to wake up. They need to wrest control back from corrupt politicians. Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest.”
The US midterm elections are seen as a turning point in the conflict – not because of their potential outcome, but because of what Trump might do after the vote.
Trump has suggested that he would either strike a deal with Iran or return to a full-scale war after the November 3 legislative elections. He has also dismissed the idea that the vote will have any impact on his Iran policy.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election. When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
If the Democrats gain control of Congress, they can push for measures to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war, including through withholding funding for the military campaign.
But Toossi said there is a debate within Iran on the potential impact of a Democratic victory in November.
While some point to foreign policy hawks among the Democrats to argue that little would change, others say a midterm defeat would make him politically vulnerable and likely constrain his war powers.
“I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Third Corps posts footage of first strike on Russia's new Dragon thermobaric weapon system

Third Corps posts footage of first strike on Russia's new Dragon thermobaric weapon system – video
Soldiers from the 3rd Army Corps have struck a Russian TOS-3 Drakon (Dragon) thermobaric rocket launcher system for the first time. The system was hit by a drone.
Source: 3rd Army Corps on social media
Details: The Drakon was struck during Operation Vivaldi. The weapon, classified as a heavy flamethrower system by the Russians, was hit by a drone operated by the Muramasa unit from the Kraken Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment.
The system was attacked 12 kilometres from the line of contact after the Drakon had been observed firing.
The attack on the Russian TOS-3 Drakon thermobaric rocket launcher system
"We have struck a Russian TOS-3 Drakon heavy flamethrower system for the first time – the enemy's latest development. This is yet another result of the 3rd Corps' systematic efforts to destroy enemy weapons and weaken its combat capabilities," the 3rd Army Corps commented on the strike.
According to the 3rd Army Corps, the TOS-3 Drakon is the latest development in the heavy flamethrower system family, which includes the Solntsepyok and TOS-2 Tosochka. The new model is equipped with slat armour and explosive reactive armour.
The system fires unguided thermobaric rockets from 15 launch tubes. The TOS-3 Drakon has an estimated range of 15 km and needs a crew of three.
