articles.title: EU leaders call on all countries to stop aiding Russia in its war against Ukraine – European Council meeting
articles.body:
European Union leaders have called on all countries to immediately cease any assistance to Russia in its war against Ukraine.
"The European Council reiterates its call on all countries to immediately cease any assistance to Russia in its war of aggression against Ukraine, whether direct or indirect, and notably through the provision of dual-use goods and components," according to the conclusions adopted following the European Council meeting held on October 15-16 in Brussels.
In particular, the European Council strongly condemns the deployment of DPRK military forces in the war against Ukraine, as well as the ongoing military support provided to Russia by, among others, Iran, Belarus, and the DPRK.
In addition, the leaders affirmed that the EU "remains committed to ensuring full accountability for war crimes and the other most serious crimes committed in connection with Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and fully supports ongoing efforts within the framework of the Council of Europe towards the operationalisation of the International Claims Commission for Ukraine and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine," the conclusions state.
The European Council also called on Russia and Belarus "to immediately ensure the safe and unconditional return to Ukraine of all unlawfully deported and transferred Ukrainian children and other civilians."
At the same time, the European Council acknowledged "the importance of the extension of temporary protection for displaced persons from Ukraine until March 2028."
"The European Union remains committed to supporting Ukraine's repair, recovery and reconstruction, in coordination with international partners, including in the areas of demining assistance and psychological and psychosocial rehabilitation," the document reads.

articles.title: US move to restart direct flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump move to restart direct US flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.
Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.
While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Trump's order "a significant first step toward restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States."
However, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Beirut-Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system.
The findings, which two senior industry officials familiar with the matter expect to delay the resumption of service, complicate efforts to follow up on an order Trump signed after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. Washington has backed Aoun as it pushes for Iran-backed Hezbollah to be disarmed.
The agency sent its internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September.
AIRPORT LACKS EMERGENCY PLAN: ICAO
Beirut airport's firefighting resources are equipped for single-aisle planes, but not twin-aisle jetliners used for long-haul flights, according to a summary of ICAO's report. The airport also lacks an emergency plan, and its conditional certification has expired, the report said.
"This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status," the summary said.
The report also found the Lebanese regulator LCAA lacks qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing, and has no fully established, operational and independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined roles.
Such concerns were flagged during a two-day workshop last month where officials from ICAO, Lebanon's government, the FAA and others discussed efforts to revive direct air service, according to the industry officials and an agenda of the meeting seen by Reuters.
Lebanon's Minister of Public Works and Transport Fayez Rasamny said Lebanon was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport starting on Saturday. The LCAA expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days.
"Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA, and corrective action had already been initiated," Rasamny said in a statement, adding that progress had been delayed by war.
Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon and have continued strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June between Israel and Lebanon.
Hezbollah, which was not party to the deal, has rejected it.
The FAA declined to comment. ICAO said it cannot comment on matters concerning specific countries, but said it conducts targeted analyses for member states.
The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Lebanon given safety concerns. It said the FAA advises caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace due to heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risks of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory.
MIDDLE EAST UNREST DISRUPTS AIR TRAVEL
Foreign airlines have avoided large swathes of Middle East airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February triggered regional hostilities, with an airport in Saudi Arabia the latest site to come under attack.
Lebanon and its national carrier have been praised domestically for maintaining air navigation services and flights, helping to prop up an economy that depends on tourism and remittances.
Reuters reported, citing three US airline officials on the condition of anonymity, they do not think any American carriers would resume flights to Lebanon in the near term due to security concerns.
While there are no direct flights between Beirut and the United States, such service exists between Lebanon and some large European cities.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and added that EU airlines must conduct their own assessment of an airport's safety and operational readiness before launching services.

articles.title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AI
articles.body:
There is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed in China and handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.
Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.
In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.
The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They are cheaper than other EVs sold in the UK and, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.
Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level.
It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.
Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last century in Tiananmen Square.
A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule.
Then came AI and the state discovered complete control.
Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to.
Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished.
For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world.
Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigorated belt and road initiative creates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology.
Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions.
Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights.
Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents.
There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers.
In practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need.
Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, as many AI experts have documented. But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option.
As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation.
He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.”
An evaluation report by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship.
“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says.
The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities.
Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assume data inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state.
The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers.
Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.

articles.title: 'Putin feels joy' — Zelensky calls Trump's waiving of key Russia sanctions 'wrong'
articles.body:
'Putin feels joy' — Zelensky calls Trump's waiving of key Russia sanctions 'wrong'
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 17 that U.S. President Donald Trump was "wrong" to further "block" sanctions against Russia, while expressing hope that the U.S. leader would do "everything possible" to stop the war.
Zelensky's comments came after Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
"Unfortunately, I don't think this is a way to stop (Russian President Vladimir) Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy that he has such support," Zelensky told reporters.
He described bipartisan support for the Russia sanction bill in September as "a major victory," calling the decision to "scrap" it "wrong."
The bill, which Trump signed weeks earlier, allows the U.S. president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas, among other measures. Trump said he would use these powers if necessary to help end Russia's war against Ukraine
Zelensky said it is likely that Washington will continue to ease sanctions on Moscow, adding that the diesel deal was "only the first step" and that further moves could follow.
"We very much hope, and I personally hope, that the U.S. president will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he added. "But once again, this can't be achieved by restricting Ukraine's response to Russia for killing our people."
"This certainly does not stop the war," the president added.
Trump's move came amid growing U.S. pressure on Ukraine to halt the attacks on Russian oil refineries. Washington has reportedly threatened to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support, while blaming the strikes for rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by energy experts.

articles.title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains
articles.body:
The United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter the Yemen conflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.
The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign that the deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed – if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.
Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.
Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations inside Yemen in January, cutting off its funding supply line.
Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.
The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.
Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.
There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.
UAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, the Houthis are determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.
On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.
The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.
The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.
Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.
In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.
The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.
Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.
No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Russia sanctions relief could continue, diesel deal ‘first step’
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that easing of US sanctions against Russia could continue, describing the recent diesel deal as only the “first step,” the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported.
Speaking to journalists, Zelenskyy said sanctions relief would give Russian President Vladimir Putin a sense of support rather than persuade him to end the war.
His comment came after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Zelenskyy, however, expressed hope that Trump "will do everything in his power" to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and end the war.
He said Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this week, stressing that Kyiv remained committed to negotiations.
He said Washington was working on a proposal for a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Russia.
Possible venues included the US at the Group of 20 summit, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia or a European country. No confirmation had yet been received from Moscow or Washington, he said.
On alleged Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy said terminals in Ukraine disconnect at speeds above about 161 kph, affecting interceptor drones targeting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones and food deliveries to isolated Ukrainian positions. He said tests in some European countries showed connections remained active at speeds exceeding 180 kph.
He said military officials, the Defense Ministry and diplomats were involved in ongoing discussions, but SpaceX had not been engaging with the military.
“At various levels, it is being claimed that these are technical issues. However, these technical issues exist in Ukraine, while they do not occur within the territory of the EU,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that European countries were exploring alternatives to Starlink after recognizing that US-based access could be restricted.
On frozen Russian assets, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had information that Moscow could seek to recover some of them through partner countries. He said he had discussed the risk with Belgium and EU leaders, adding that the assets remained under European control and were secure.
European partners opposed the US-Russian diesel deal and agreed that sanctions should remain in place while Russia continued its attacks, Zelenskyy said, adding that work on another sanctions package was also underway.

articles.title: Trump Says He Would Like to See Putin at G20 Summit
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said he is uncertain whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will attend the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami this December, but stated that he “would love to have him” at the gathering.
Responding to questions from journalists regarding Putin’s prospective participation, Trump confirmed that the Russian leader’s attendance remains unconfirmed, Forbes TV News reported on Saturday, Oct. 17.

“I don’t know if he’s coming. I would love to have him, certainly,” Trump told reporters.
The remarks follow earlier statements from the White House indicating an openness to hosting the Russian leader at the multilateral summit, which is scheduled to convene in Florida in December.
The prospective invitation has emerged as a point of contention among Western allies and European institutions, who have maintained an international diplomatic boycott of the Russian head of state since the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
President Trump:
"I don't know" if Putin will be attending G-20 Summit in Miami pic.twitter.com/aT4FTQ8dVZ
— Forbes Breaking News (@ForbesTVNews) October 16, 2026
European pushback
Trump’s openness to hosting Putin in Miami has drawn sharp criticism from European officials.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas previously condemned the diplomatic invitation, pointing to state-sponsored security threats and criminal indictments unsealed in the US involving Russian intelligence operations.
Kallas highlighted a September indictment by the US Department of Justice charging individuals linked to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) with plotting the contract assassination of a prominent Russian dissident on American soil.
Trump Denies Role in Slowing Ukraine’s Military Starlink
“Trump’s inviting Putin to the G20 was very hard to hear,” Kallas stated, arguing that hostile intelligence activities operate under direct instructions from the Kremlin.
The European Commission confirmed that the EU will use the Miami summit to condemn Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine, regardless of whether Putin travels to the event.
Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill emphasized that the 27-nation bloc has utilized every G20 platform since 2022 to demand the cessation of hostilities, reiterating that the stance will continue “irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”
Any potential international travel by Putin also intersects with legal obligations surrounding the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023 over unlawful deportations of Ukrainian children.
While the US is not a state party to the Rome Statute of the ICC and is not legally obligated under treaty law to execute ICC warrants, an in-person appearance by Putin would mark his first visit to a Western nation since the full-scale war began.
Kremlin positioning
The Kremlin has responded cautiously to public discussions regarding the Florida summit, sending mixed signals regarding whether Putin would accept an official US invitation.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov previously described speculation regarding Putin’s travel as “premature,” noting that an official determination has not yet been finalized by the presidential administration.
Peskov also dismissed prospects for a prospective bilateral encounter between Putin and President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the Miami meeting, reiterating Moscow’s stance that any substantive leader-level consultations could occur only in the Russian capital.

articles.title: Defence Forces strike facility in Russia's Rostov region, MTZ depot of Russian missile brigade – General Staff
articles.body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) confirmed that on October 16, a production and warehouse building belonging to Roboavia company was struck near the town of Lenina in Russia's Rostov region.
"The strike on the infrastructure of the company, which develops and manufactures unmanned aerial vehicles for the Russian army, is aimed at disrupting the production and supply of UAVs to Russian troops," the General Staff said on its Telegram channel.
In addition, it was confirmed that on October 12, a logistics warehouse belonging to a unit of the enemy's missile brigade was struck near the village of Latyshi in Russia's Bryansk region.
"The strikes on such targets constitute Ukraine's exercise of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and are aimed at reducing the military, economic, and technological capabilities of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said.
